t: Army Receipts Book used for receipting transactions. It is always completed in triplicate.
Army Cash Book used for recording cash and bank transactions. It is usually balanced at the end of the month.

In a withdrawal operation, abandonment is the final withdrawal of the last elements of troops from a position. The time for the final abandonment is one of the key timings given in a withdrawal operation.
To terminate a mission for any reason other than enemy action. It may occur at any point after the beginning of the mission and prior to its completion.
A trial or test carried out by nominated representative of the eventual military users of a weapon or equipment to determine if specific performance and characteristics have been met.
Intelligence derived from the collection and processing of acoustic (sound-related) phenomena.
To perform the duties of a given rank or appointment.
Any device which has to radiate to gain information, either for surveillance or for target engagement, e.g., radar, searchlight and infra-red devices.

An address group is a group of 3 random letters assigned to disguise or conceal a command, formation, unit or sub-unit on a radio net. The first letter of an address group should not begin with the letter Q or Z as these are used in other procedure. Address group is used as a temporary call sign, when a station joins a net for which he has no allocated call sign.
Adjustment is the process by which an observer brings fire to bear on a target by ordering corrections to the observed fall of shot(s).

Adjutant is the principal staff officer in the command cell of a battlegroup who assumes the co-ordination role, if the Second-in-Command is otherwise employed. He is responsible for the allocation and control of real estate in the battlegroup area of operations; this includes co-ordinating the requirements of other units and detachments which may be temporarily located in the area and which may be under TACON. He is also responsible for the continuous update and execution of the Surveillance and Target Acquisition Plan (STAP) and for the production of movement orders.

Administration covers the management and execution of all military matters not included in tactics and strategy; primarily in the fields of logistics and personnel management. It is the internal management of units both in peace and in war.

An area where admin units and unit admin echelons are located and from where they carry out their functions. It may involve offloading transport but does not hold dumped stocks in excess of the formation's second line holdings.

Direction or exercise of authority over subordinate or other organisations in respect to administrative matters such as personnel management, supply, services, and other matters not included in the operational missions of the subordinate or other organisations.

A written order produced at formation level and above covering traffic, supply, maintenance, evacuation, personnel and other administrative detail designed to:
a. Give the necessary administrative information to formations and units being supplied.
b. Give essential detail and information to the administrative services so that they can carry out allotted tasks.
A plan normally relating to and complementing an operation plan or order, which provides information and instruction covering the logistical and administrative support of the operation.

1. A verbal command to move forward.

2. An offensive operation that is categorised into:
a. Advance to Contact. An offensive operation designed to gain or re-establish contact with the enemy.
b. Advance in Contact. An offensive operation that is aimed at maintaining the contact that was already made with the enemy covering force, intermediate positions or main defensive position. A commander should be prepared to take a certain degree of risk.
c. Pursuit. Pursuit is an offensive operation aimed at destroying or fatally disrupting a retreating or withdrawing enemy force.
A base located in or near an area of operation when it is not possible to maintain the force directly from the main base.

A moving body of troops of about a battle group size that protects the head of a larger body (a brigade strength and above) from attack. It is also responsible for gaining information on the enemy and ground. Advance guard has 2 groups:
a. Vanguard. That part of the advance guard that protects the main guard. It is based on a company group.
b. Main Guard. Advance guard less the Vanguard.

ASC is set up to reinforce Main Dressing Station (MDS) with field surgical and transfusion team in a situation where the 6-hour target to evac casualties from MDS to Field Hospital cannot be met. This is to give the MDS the capability for performing surgery.
The opponent in a military operation. An enemy or a warring party in a conflict in which the Alliance has direct involvement as in Warfighting.
The normal relationship of direct support artillery with its supported arm which results in the best possible cooperation between the supporting and the supported arms.
A distinct non-military body which has objectives that are broadly consistent with those of the campaign.
An agent is a person specifically recruited, trained and infiltrated into a hostile organisation with the task of gaining and reporting information about its activities.

ADC is a personal appointment assigned to (commanding) general officers of 2-star rank or appointment and above. The main duty of the ADC is to arrange for the personal and social requirements of his commander. He is also responsible for the security of his commander (and his family in peacetime). He should be a combatant officer.

1. A single unambiguous military purpose that must be established before a plan can be developed at any level of command for a military operation.

2. In service papers, 'aim' is a separate heading that enables the reader to see immediately whether the paper is designed to meet his requirements and to see if the writer is straying into irrelevancies. The aim should follow directly from the setting given in the introduction, and should be as short as possible and should also state whether or not recommendations are to be made. The aim always begins with the words 'The aim of this paper is to...' and should be single and not multiple; e.g., 'to assess', and not 'to state and explain'. The aim should be qualified only by those limitations that have been imposed by superior authority and are completely outside your discretion.

An air campaign is defined as a coordinated series of air operations designed to achieve a specific air strategic objective. There are 3 types of Air Campaign: the Counter-Air Campaign, the Anti-Surface Force Campaign and the Strategic Air Offensive.

A team specially organised to direct close air support in the vicinity of forward ground elements by visual and other means. The team normally consists of an air force officer - Forward Air Controller (FAC) and a Ground Liaison Officer.
A space where helicopters and FGA can operate tactically, i.e. close to the ground. It must be clear of obstructions such as power lines, towers, radio masts, etc.
Active or passive measures taken to nullify or reduce the effectiveness of attack by hostile aircraft or guided missiles against ground forces, installations, etc.

A designated area of airspace and/or ground territory within which specific air defence measures are established and coordinated to detect, identify, intercept or neutralise hostile aerial threats.
1. ADA CLASS A. Area prohibited to friendly aircraft.
2. ADA CLASS B. Area with certain specified restrictions.
3. ADA CLASS C. Complete freedom of action for friendly aircraft within the area.

A branch of artillery concerned primarily with:
a. The provision of close defence of ground targets against low altitude enemy air attack by destructive fire.
b. The provision of a deterrent fire to prevent enemy aircraft from penetrating or passing over an area at low altitude.

The highest level in an air defence organization where overall command of the air situation is exercised. Information provided by the lower elements in the system includes processed data, weapons states, force deployment and readiness data.

The control of air defence weapons is exercised by the following orders:

Weapons Free. Air defence systems may engage any target not positively identified as friendly.

Weapons Hold. Air defence systems may only engage in self-defence or in response to a formal order.

Weapons Tight. Air defence systems may engage a target only if it is positively identified as hostile.

Weapons Unlimited. No restrictions on engagement. This order is used only in the specific circumstance when a Hostile Aircraft Free Engagement Zone (HAFEZ) has been declared.
Delivery of personnel or cargo from airborne aircraft.
AI is a deep operation conducted to destroy, disrupt, neutralise or delay the enemy's military potential before it can be brought to bear effectively against friendly forces.
Communication link used for liaison on air matters between the Air Liaison Officer's cell at formation HQ and the appropriate NAF HQ.

The air force officer in charge of the air force support cell at formation HQ. At brigade level he is referred to as the Brigade Air Liaison Officer (BALO) while at divisional level, he is the Divisional Air Liaison Officer (DALO).

Air Manoeuvre Forces exploit the mobility of aircraft to provide reach and agility. Air manoeuvre forces include attack, support and reconnaissance helicopters; air assault and airborne infantry; combat support and combat service support elements. Their operations should be closely integrated with close air support and air interdiction.
Any number of aircraft sorties dispatched simultaneously on a particular task.
A combat force which moves above battlefield in air vehicles under the control of a ground force commander in order to engage in ground combat.

In the execution of an air move, the air mounting centre is a suitable transit camp or barracks near the departure airfield where troops, vehicles and equipment are assembled into chalks and air portability procedures, safety requirements and documentation are carried out. Troops are also briefed here. Good communication is required between the AMC and the airfield. The security of the area must be good to enable briefing of troops for operations to take place in secrecy.

A table produced by a joint planning conference which precedes any air move, showing the airlift available for the operation. A table is prepared for each type of aircraft to show:
a. The departure and destination aircraft.
b. The allocation of individual aircraft to the formation by chalk numbers.
c. The payload available (or the internal configuration) of each aircraft.
d. Flight details.

An elevated observation post, operated and controlled by the army, from which aerial observation is carried out. It normally consists of a light unarmed aircraft flown by an artillery officer; under the operational control of the appropriate artillery HQ and operating at low altitude behind own forward troops.
Neither side can guarantee air dominance.
Air portable denotes materials which can be conveniently carried by aircraft either internally or externally with only minor dismantling and reassembling all within the capabilities of user units.
Reconnaissance from the air. The quickest and most reliable source of intelligence in war. Generally includes photographic, visual, infra-red line scan, radar and use of electronic sensors.
The message sent by a unit/formation to the air force requesting for close air support, interdiction or air reconnaissance.

The basic planning document for an air prepared down to unit level. It shows the details of men, vehicles, guns, equipment and stores which would be taken by air. These details provide the basis on which number and types of aircraft to lift the unit or formation can be estimated.
The carriage by air of all types of equipment and stores.

The principal air support agency at Corps HQ commanded by an Air Liaison Officer (ALO), normally the Wg Comd Ops. Air support responsibilities may be differentiated by breaking down the ASOC into cells for easy control. For example, Offensive Support (OS), Air Transport (AT), etc., as required.
That degree of a Favourable Air Situation or Air Superiority where the opposing air force is incapable of effective interference.
Army officer with a small staff attached to each transport airfield to provide liaison between army units moving by air and the air force staff at the departure and arrival airfields.

An airborne operation is an operation involving the movement of combat forces and their logistic support into an objective area by air. Airborne forces may be inserted by parachute, either directly onto the objective or onto adjacent drop zones; they may be self-supporting for short-term operations, or the operations may call for additional combat support and CSS units.
The capacity of an aircraft expressed as a weight.

A designated area in a hostile or threatened territory which, when seized and held, ensures the continuous air landing of troops and materiel and provides the manoeuvre space necessary for projected operation. Normally it is the area seized in the assault phase of an airborne operation.

The purpose of airspace control is to balance two conflicting requirements: the need to optimise air defence protection and the need to allow aircraft freedom to operate with the minimum restrictions.

Alarm post is a temporary fire position which may be occupied, if fire trenches are not ready, and alarm is raised. Arms, ammunition and equipment are kept ready, at hand, at the alarm post. Alarm posts generally correspond to the number of the fire trenches and are situated near them.
A defensive position is said to be sited for all-round defence when weapons are so located as to bring an equal volume of fire in all directions upon attack.
All Stations Call is a type of call used when it is essential to call all the stations on a net. Unless a reply is essential, all stations calls will end with the proword 'OUT'.

An earmarked position to be occupied when it becomes necessary to vacate a present position. The concept of a force occupying one of a number of positions will depend on the ability to move from the position to another when under air attack, direct or indirect fire. Alternate positions provide additional lines of sight into the same killing area similar to that of the primary position. They increase the survivability of a weapons system by enabling it to engage the enemy in one engagement area from multiple positions. A weapons system may fire one or two rounds from each position before moving to the next position to complicate enemy target acquisition. Alternate positions should be designated and prepared as time permits.
A position adjacent to the primary one, still covering the primary arc, to which a tank may jockey as required.

A surprise attack by fire from concealed positions on a moving or temporarily halted enemy. The purpose of an ambush is to inflict damage on the enemy while denying him an opportunity to counter-attack, principally through surprise.
A device charged with explosives, propellants, pyrotechnics, initiating composition, or nuclear, biological or chemical material for use in connection with defence or offence, including demolitions.
Any vehicle that swims (not to be confused with Fording).
An amphibious operation is an operation launched from the sea by naval and landing forces against a hostile or potentially hostile shore.

In intelligence usage, a step in the processing phase of the Intelligence Cycle in which information or intelligence is subjected to review in order to identify significant facts for subsequent interpretation. See also "Intelligence Cycle".
A static OP who engages targets, in order to provide covering fire to attacking troops.
Supplementary document that amplifies a parent document. Annexes are used when the inclusion of all details in the body of the parent document would make it cumbersome.

AAI is an annual inspection of units/HQ, which is aimed at providing the appropriate commander with detailed information concerning the units/HQ on which to assess its fitness to carry out its role. AAI also provides an avenue to offer help and advice in order to resolve any difficulties.
In operational art, anticipation is the key to effective planning so as to remain alert for the unexpected and for opportunities to exploit the situation.
A mine primarily designed to be initiated by the presence, proximity or contact of a person.
A supplementary document that amplifies an annex.

Titles used to refer to officers in command and to other holders of service appointments. Although appointment titles have no security in themselves, they disguise the level at which the appointment is held, e.g., Sunray, meaning Commander at any level. Other appointment titles are as follows:
a. 2 iC - SUNRAY MINOR.
b. Adjutant - SEAGULL.
c. Admin Staff - MAN HOLE.
d. Quarter Master - MOLAR.
e. Armour Rep - IRONSIDE.
f. Army Avn Rep - HAWK EYE.
g. Arty Rep - SHELDRAKE.
h. COAS - MOON BEAM.
i. Commander - SUNRAY.
j. Engr Rep - HOLD FAST.
k. EME Rep - BLUE BELL.
l. Grd Liaison Offr - GLOW WARM.
m. Inf Rep - FOX HOUND.
n. Int Rep - ACORN.
o. Locating Arty - CRACKER.
p. Med Rep - STARLIGHT.
q. Nig Civil Police - KEY STONE.
r. Ord Rep - RICKSHAW.
s. Prov Rep - WATCH DOG.
t. Q' (CSS) Staff - NUTSHELL.
u. S & T Rep - PLAY TIME.
v. Sig Officer - PROTON.

An area of ground for which a fire unit or a weapon is responsible and within which it engages targets (arc of fire is not the same as field of fire). Arc of fire is in 2 categories:
a. Primary arc of fire. The area which is the basic responsibility of a fire unit or weapon.
b. Secondary arc of fire. A subsidiary task or responsibility of a fire unit or weapon undertaken when not engaged in its primary arc.

Area Defence focuses on the retention of terrain by absorbing the enemy into a framework of static and mutually supporting positions from which he can be largely destroyed by fire. The emphasis is on retention of terrain or its denial to the enemy for a specified time.
A geographical area wherein a commander is directly capable of influencing operations, by manoeuvre or fire support systems normally under his command or control.

That area of concern to the Commander, including the area of influence and areas occupied by enemy forces that could jeopardize the accomplishment of the mission. In order to provide the necessary information and intelligence, the G2 staff will invariably have to request it from higher, or flanking, units and formations.
The area allocated to a commander in which he is responsible for the provision of intelligence within the means at his disposal. The efforts of his G2 staff will be devoted mainly to this area.

AO is the geographical area assigned to a commander by a higher commander; it has lateral and rear boundaries which usually define it within a larger geographical area. Within these limits, a commander has the authority to conduct operations, co-ordinate fire, control movement, develop and maintain installations. His authority should include the control of all joint actions supporting his mission.
AOR defines the geographical area associated with a command within which a commander has authority to plan and conduct operations as delegated.
Reconnaissance conducted by recce forces to obtain information about a given area, e.g., a town, a ridge line, woods or other features that may be critical to an operation.
A soldier given the responsibility of storing, maintaining and accounting for the unit weapons, e.g., small arms, mortars, etc.

Vehicle from where the commander of a mechanized force exercises command over his forces. It is configured with enough radios for all nets and working space for staff work. It is usually based on a modified APC.
A tracked or wheeled armoured combat land vehicle primarily designed for offensive purposes but which may be used for other specialist purposes.

Refers to an infantry/armour force composition where armour is in the majority. Manpower is not the deciding factor but the numbers of the formations, units or subunits contributed by either to the force. Vice versa is the case with regards to Infantry Predominant or Infantry Heavy.
Armoured vehicle designed for the recovery of tanks and other armoured fighting vehicles including armoured personnel carriers.
A bridge laying tank with limited capability for the crossing of gaps of about 50 feet in width. It is essential for the maintenance of momentum and is organic to the battalion.

Air wing of an army used primarily for the transportation of forces and material. Army Aviation does not include fighters or bombers as those belong to the air force, but may include helicopters of all kinds.

The role of army engineers is to provide close support to the battlegroup. This will include the provision of timely and effective mobility, counter mobility, survivability support and, where necessary, the provision of general engineer support.

An army unit organized to provide for reinforcement of personnel and the replacement of armoured fighting vehicles and other equipment in the combat zone. The unit is of a battalion status with companies at divisional level and platoons at brigade level.
The climax of an attack; closing with the enemy in hand-to-hand fighting.

An area in which a command is assembled for final administrative preparation or regrouping of battalions and company groups preparatory to further action. It should be:
a. Free from enemy ground observation.
b. Concealed from enemy visual air recce.
c. Easily accessible.
d. Preferably out of range of enemy mortars.
e. Have sufficient space.
The extension of visibility which allows the location and state of individual serially numbered or uniquely identified items to be determined when required.

A precedence applied to the task of an artillery unit to provide fire to a formation/unit on a guaranteed basis. Normally observer, communications and liaison are not provided. An artillery unit in "direct support" or "in support" may simultaneously be placed "at priority call" to another unit or agency for a specific period of time.

An offensive action or operation of war which culminates in the capture of an objective, the destruction of an enemy force or the directing of enemy's attention from other areas of operation. Attack may be:
a. Quick Attack. An attack against hastily prepared enemy defences and aimed at gaining a measure of surprise. It is characterized by quick appreciation, map recce by junior commanders with time for procedure reduced to a minimum. Orders are usually issued on radio.
b. Deliberate Attack. This is the same as a coordinated attack (see "Coordinated Attack"), usually launched against well-coordinated enemy defences. It is characterised by detailed ground recce, planning down to the lowest level of command and co-ordinated employment of fire power and manoeuvre to close with and destroy or capture the enemy position.
Fire employed to destroy the enemy from a distance, which is normally used when the mission does not dictate or support occupation of the objective.

The AGM is a matrix which lists enemy targets in order of priority with guidance as to when, and by what means, the targets should be attacked. It also details the desired effect to be achieved (destroy/neutralise).
Attrition is the reduction of the effectiveness of a force caused by loss of personnel and materiel.

A style of warfare characterized by the application of substantial combat power that reduces an enemy's ability to fight through loss of personnel and equipment. Essentially it aims at the physical destruction of the enemy.
Authentication procedures are a COMSEC aid designed to prevent the enemy from infiltrating a radio net, and to allow stations to prove that they are genuine.

The authorised commander is the commander who has the authority to order the firing of a reserved demolition. He may delegate this authority to a subordinate commander, in which case the subordinate becomes the authorised commander.
An AA is two or more mobility corridors (see "mobility corridor") running in the same direction and belonging to the next lower level of command.
In land warfare, axis is the general line astride which a force moves. It is a line drawn on a map usually between assigned boundaries to indicate the general direction of advance.

Back-brief is the brief carried out by subordinate commanders to their superior commander and fellow commanders on their own plans after receiving orders if time and circumstances permit. It is not designed to seek approval for a plan but rather to increase mutual knowledge in, and understanding of, each other's plans.
The rearward movement of equipment, casualties and materiel within a theatre of operation.

In operational art, balance is an appropriate mix of forces and capabilities within the joint force. It is made up of elements that are complementary to each other to enable that force function as a team. A balanced force is said to be of:
a. Balanced Composition. When it contains the correct proportion of the various arms and services as required by the conditions of ground and enemy.
b. Balanced Disposition. When the various elements of the force are so deployed to enable the commander retain the initiative and be capable of reacting decisively to any enemy action, even off the line of march.

A moving belt of fire providing a screen behind which attacking troops advance. Uneconomical in guns and ammunition. The aim is to neutralize the enemy on ground over which own infantry and armour will pass. It also assists advancing troops to maintain direction and the correct rate of advance.

A co-ordinated series of obstacles designed or employed to detect, channel, direct, restrict, delay or stop the movement of an opposing force, and to impose additional losses in personnel, time and equipment on the opposing force.

An area declared by an authorized commander where manoeuvre of friendly forces must not be hindered by barriers. Restrictions imposed may include a complete ban on the emplacement of obstacles in certain areas for specified periods.

a. A locality from which operations are projected or supported.
b. An area or locality containing installations which provide logistic or other support. It is normally synonymous with Fourth Line, i.e., the CSS provided from the base organisation.

In CRW, Base Area is the area, virtually free from guerrilla interference, that has a defensive perimeter, and from which offensive operations may be mounted and supported. It will normally be based on a port and/or strategic transport terminal airfield.
Ordnance unit affiliated on a scale of one per division, to provide ordnance support. A measure of control is still retained by the Director Ordnance Services.

1. A small area of level ground surrounded or nearly surrounded by hills.
2. A district drained by a river and its tributaries, for example, the basin of the Niger.
3. A depression in the Earth's surface that contains water.

Temporary bases set up when establishing or expanding control areas. Such bases may be located alongside civil/police HQ, near defended villages, or in the countryside. Defence arrangements must allow for a large proportion of the force to be out of the base on offensive operations.

The Second-in-Command is the CO 'in waiting' but fulfils the role of chief of staff within the HQ. He supervises the running of Main and is directly responsible to the battlegroup commander for the co-ordination and synchronisation of all current and future plans. He is responsible for the production of the Synchronisation Matrix. He monitors the battle and ensures that the battlegroup commander is informed of all recommendations made by the staff at Main. He monitors CSS within the battlegroup, particularly replenishment, defence stores and recovery, and in close liaison with the BG Log O, he ensures that all plans are logistically supportable. He ensures that all regrouped sub units are properly briefed.

The BC provides artillery advice, communications and liaison to the battlegroup and he is responsible for coordinating all the battlegroup's offensive support (OS). He will be involved in all stages of the planning process and will formulate the OS fire plan to reflect the battlegroup commander's Concept of Operations.
The day on which deployment for an operation commences or is due to commence.

The internal diameter of the bore of a gun, pistol, mortar or rifle and also the diameter of a round. It is expressed in inches, centimetres or millimetres, as the case may be, e.g., 105mm main gun of the Eagle tank and the common 7.62mm NATO ammunition of the FN rifle.
Figures, letters, or combination of both, used to identify a communications station, an organization, or an individual on a radio net. Its primary use is to establish and maintain communications.
A tactical task used to restrict operations to a narrow zone by the use of obstacles, fire, or unit manoeuvring or positioning.
Operation consisting of taking one or more spare parts from repairable or fit equipment to respond to an urgent supply need.

Camouflage is the use of natural or artificial material on personnel, objects or tactical positions with the aim of confusing, misleading or evading the enemy. It is the process of making a person or object blend with its background.
CASS is an equipment based on flexible fibreglass rods, to replace conventional methods of supporting camouflage nets. It is issued as part of the concealment sets for all high value equipments.

A campaign is a sequence of planned, resourced and executed joint military operations designed to achieve a strategic objective within a given time and space, more usually involving the synchronization of land, sea and air forces.
To capture is to seize or gain possession of a position or terrain, with or without the use of force.
Casualty covers sick/wounded personnel, malfunctioned and damaged equipment, including vehicles.

The process of collecting, sorting, treating and evacuating the sick and wounded. It is designed to:
a. Remove casualty as quickly as possible from units to allow those units retain their mobility.
b. Evacuate casualties as far from the battle area as is necessary to enable effective treatment to be carried out.

A type of tactical movement used during mechanised and non-mechanised operations. The movement itself is similar to a live caterpillar. The rear tanks/APCs/troops cover the movement of the forward tanks/APCs/troops with fire until the next bound or fire position is reached. The rear tanks/APCs/troops then move forward to join the leading tanks/APCs/troops, and the process is repeated.

This manoeuvre allows time for the leading tanks/APCs/troops to view the ground they will advance over and ensures that the same set of eyes are viewing the front at all times. It is, however, slower than Leap Frogging (see "Leap Frogging").

Caterpillaring is employed when enemy contact is imminent or expected.
Process of vetting information or material. Part or portion of information or material that is determined as injurious or damaging is prevented from passing.
A depot established to hold army reserve stocks. It is directly controlled by the corps commander of the service concerned, e.g., Central Ordnance Depot Yaba (CODY), Lagos.
An imaginary line, route or alignment along which HQ moves in the advance.
In operational art, COGs are those characteristics, capabilities, or locations from which a military force derives its freedom of action, physical strength, or will to fight.

A load of troops in an aircraft identified by a particular chalk Number. A 'Chalk Number' is the number given to a complete aircraft load and the aircraft carrying it. An aircraft will have a different chalk number for each successive sortie.

1. Process of arraigning an accused.
2. The rush to seize enemy position in the assault. 'Charge' is also used as a battle cry.
3. Charge magazine to make a rifle already loaded and having a round in the chamber, safe rather than by application of safety catch.
4. Charge battery to raise specific gravity level of a weak battery.
5. The explosive content of any device.

A demolition on which all charges have been placed and which is at one of the states of readiness below:
a. State of Readiness '1' (SAFE). The demolition charge has been placed and secured. The vertical and horizontal ring mains are disconnected and the detonators are not inserted in the two initiating sets.
b. State of Readiness '2' (ARMED). Demolition is ready for immediate firing.

A pre-determined point used as a means of controlling movement. In a withdrawal, it is normally established at an easily recognizable location on the route back from the defensive position through which troops move on their way back to the RV. A physical count of forces withdrawing is made. Forces do not halt at a check point.

A chemical substance intended for use in military operations to kill, seriously injure or incapacitate man through its physiological effects. Riot control agents, chemical herbicides, smoke and flame are not considered as chemical agents. When employed operationally, the form of warfare in that theatre is chemical warfare/operation.

A Chemical Operation is the employment of chemical agents to kill, injure, or incapacitate, for a significant period of time, man or animals, and deny or hinder the use of areas, facilities or materiel, or defence against such employment.

The most senior staff officer in a HQ at brigade level and above. He advises the commander on all matters, implements his policy and in the absence of the commander takes decisions on his behalf. He coordinates all aspects of work in the HQ.
The term 'Civil Authorities' covers local authorities, such as magistrates and police forces, District and County Councils and central government.

Civil Defence are volunteer civilian population assigned to specific tasks for the protection and survival of the civilian population during the war or national disaster. The specific civil defence tasks provided for by the law of war include:
a. Provision of warning systems.
b. Evacuation of the wounded.
c. Construction of shelter.
d. Rescue operations.
e. Medical services, including first aid.
f. Religious assistance.
g. Fire fighting.
h. Detection and marking of danger areas.
i. Decontamination and similar protective measures.
j. Provision of emergency accommodation and supplies.
k. Emergency assistance in the restoration and maintenance of order in distressed areas.
l. Emergency repair of indispensable public utilities.
m. Emergency disposal of the dead.
n. Assistance in preservation of objects essential for survival.
o. Complementary activities necessary to carry out any of the tasks mentioned above, including, but not limited to planning and organization.
Active or passive resistance of the civil population to the authority or policies of a government, by such means embark on unlawful strikes.
Group acts of violence and disorder prejudicial to public law and order. These will necessitate police and possible military intervention.

CIMIC is defined as the resources and arrangements which support the relationship between commanders and national authorities, civil and military, and civil populations in an area where military forces are, or plan to be employed. Such measures include cooperation with non-governmental or international agencies.
All objects which are not military objectives.

Civilian persons means any person who do not belong to the Armed Forces and do not take part in a "levee en masse". In case of doubt whether a person is a civilian or not, that person shall be considered a civilian. Journalists engaged in dangerous professional mission in areas of armed conflict are civilian persons.

Activities sponsored or by government department or agencies in such a way as to maintain secrecy by concealment or stealth, i.e., concealed but not disguised. They differ from covert operations which lay emphasis on disguised but not concealed.

EME repairs are classified as follows:
a. Unit Repairs. Minor adjustments or the replacement of components and minor assemblies. This requires only hand tools, a limited amount of machinery and portable test equipment.
b. Field Repairs. Repairs requiring more time and workshop facilities than a unit repair, such as the repair of major assemblies.
c. Intermediate Repairs. Repairs beyond the category of a field repair but which does not justify the complete rebuild of an equipment or assembly carried out in Base Workshops.
d. Base Repairs. The complete overhaul or rebuild of equipment and assemblies to an 'as-new' condition.

EME support are classified as follows:
a. First line Support. Organic unit EME backing like LADS and unit workshops attached to units holding specialist equipment, e.g., workshop supporting divisional engineers.
b. Second line Support. Fully mobile infantry and armoured workshops which support infantry and armoured brigade respectively.
c. Third line Support. Generally, corresponds to intermediate repairs within a division, provided by the base workshop.
d. Fourth line Support. Generally, corresponds to base repairs provided by central workshops, artillery base workshop and engineer base workshop.
e. Electronic Repairs. The army signals provide first and second line support to units while NAEME is responsible for base repairs.

Cleared route is the route against which enemy cannot bring direct fire to bear. It must be kept clear until handed over to another formation or unit. It is used for speedy movement of men, supply and evacuation.
Air action against hostile targets which are in close proximity to friendly forces and which require detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of those forces.

The restriction of the liberty of a person subject to military law, who is alleged to have committed an offence against that law by being placed in the charge of an escort, or in confinement sometimes necessarily under lock and key.
The authorized holding of clothing for a unit.

A code word is a single word with a pre-arranged meaning, used to establish a condition, an alert, or to initiate the implementation of a plan or operation. Their meanings are always classified and are intended to be used once only as an executive order. Code words are rarely used in connection with communications, other than for conditions of electronic silence.
Cohesion is the quality that binds together the constituent parts of a force thereby providing resilience against dislocation and disruption.
A neck or ridge of land connecting two mountains or hills. A col is lower than the surrounding plain or valley.

The worldwide struggle in the peacetime between communism and the free world, waged by all means short of international armed conflict. Cold war covers propaganda, subversion, economic sanctions, civil war, revolts and rebellions inspired by a basic ideological conflict.
One who during his/her period of captivity either sympathises with or actively collaborates with the enemy.

Collection plan is developed by the G2 and G3 staffs working together; it sets out how the information and intelligence needed to meet the commander's Priority Intelligence Requirements (PIRs) is to be collected.

A collective call is a type of call to two or more selected stations on a net identified by a single pre-designated collective call sign. Use of collective calls enables communication with regularly required groups of stations without the need to specify each individual call sign. Collective calls can significantly reduce the length of calling transmissions.
Combined training at section, platoon, subunit and unit level of a particular arm or service. When such training combines various arms under one commander, it becomes Group Training.
Formation or body of troops moving or deployed axially.

An aircraft patrol over a predetermined area, a designated force, a critical area of the Combat Zone, or over an air defence area for the purpose of intercepting and destroying hostile aircraft before they reach their targets. This is a defensive measure against hostile aircraft only and may not operate against a ground threat to the force protected.
The total amount of supplies required to support one day of combat, calculated by applying the intensity factor to a standard day of supply.

CE is the assessment of a unit/formation's ability to use his assets to their full potential, i.e., is it 100%, or has his potential been degraded by damage, lack of maintenance, lack of rest, etc., i.e., less than 100%.

Combat Engineering is the engineering support in the Combat Zone. It includes:
a. Construction and maintenance of roads and tracks.
b. Construction and maintenance of forward airstrips and helicopter landing points.
c. Water supply.
d. Clearing of mines and booby traps.
e. Construction of field defences.
f. Demolitions.
g. Construction of obstacles including minefields.
h. River and obstacle crossings.
Combat forces are those forces which use manoeuvre to engage the enemy with direct fire weapon systems. They are the infantry, armour and aviation.

The knowledge of the enemy, weather and geographical features required by a commander in the planning and conduct of tactical operations. Combat intelligence can be further subdivided into two types of intelligence:
a. Basic Intelligence. The general reference material for use in planning concerning enemies or potential enemies which pertains to capabilities, resources or potential theatres of operation.
b. Current Intelligence. Implies intelligence of a tactical nature and may be defined as "the daily or hourly flow of evaluated information".

This is assault order with the means of stowage for rations and personal equipment to enable a soldier to live and fight for 24 hours. In addition to assault order, the following is carried inside the second side pouch of the rucksack:
a. Two meals from the 24 hour ration pack contained in one mess tin, hexamine cooker, knife fork and spoon (KFS).
b. A pair of socks, head cover, gloves, washing and shaving kit, foot powder and other minor items.
c. One extra layer of clothing for the top half of the body.

The total means of destructive force which a military unit/formation can apply against the enemy at a given time. Combat power Can be quantified as numbers of men, weapons and equipment that are readily available during operation; it is different from fighting power. See "Fighting Power".

Combat Reconnaissance is the means by which the intelligence requirements and targeting data for forces in or near contact with the enemy is met, normally through the Close Recce Platoon/Troop. However, other elements of the battle group may be used.
Stocks of essential items held on the ground in an operational area normally within reach of second line transport for use only in an emergency.

CSS is defined as the support provided to combat elements, primarily in the fields of administration and logistics. It encompasses medical support, provost support, personnel support, logistic support, equipment support, logistic engineering support and the civilian resources provided to formations. The principles of CSS are explained below:
a. Foresight. CSS planners, at all levels, have to assess the probable course of future operations and forecast the likely requirement for personnel, medical support, materiel and equipment, including their movement.
b. Economy. CSS planners have to ensure that the most efficient use is made of the available personnel, materiel and movement facilities.
c. Simplicity. Although the support of deployed forces is a complex and detailed undertaking, the plan to provide the support must remain simple; it must not only be easy to understand but also easy to put into effect. Complicated plans not only remove the element of initiative at subordinate levels but also increase the risk and probability of confusion.
d. Cooperation. The CSS elements of a formation have to function as a team in which each element directs all of its efforts towards a Command Service Support.
e. Common goal. Close cooperation between the staff and the support units is essential. Both need to be confident that they will not be asked to satisfy unreasonable demands. This confidence can be fostered by frequent visits, close liaison, and effective coordination.
f. Flexibility. The CSS elements of a formation need to be able to conform to the commander's plans, which will almost inevitably be subject to continuous change. Therefore, the CSS organisation will need to have the capacity to adapt and to be able to adjust its efforts as required by the commander.

Combat Supplies include ammunition, POL and rations:
a. Ammunition includes conventional ammunition, mines, explosives and guided weapons.
b. POL includes petrol, oil and lubricant - all liquid fuels, lubricants and anti-freeze.
c. Rations include all food and forage. Their resupply includes associated items such as hexamine cookers, disinfectants and water purification chemicals.

Combat support forces provide fire support and operational assistance to the combat elements and are therefore essential to the conduct of operations; they are corps of artillery, engineers, signals and support helicopters.
Measures to be taken when involuntarily separated from friendly forces in combat, including procedures relating to individual survival, evasion, escape and conduct after capture.
Forces whose primary mission is the destruction of enemy forces and installations.
Light armoured fighting vehicle suited for the reconnaissance role and which retains a limited anti-armour capacity to enable it fight for information or extrication, e.g., Scorpion.

The forward part of the theatre of operations near to the enemy where the main combat forces are located. The Combat Zone is subdivided into:
a. Corps Area. The replenishment park is established in this area and could hold up to 3 days of supplies. If Combat Reserve areas are established, it could hold 4-7 days supplies.
b. Division Administrative Area (DAA). As DAA is far forward only 2-3 days of supplies are normally held.
c. Brigade Administrative Area (BAA). 2 days of supplies are held in the BAA.

In the teaching of 'Law of War', "Combatants" means members of the armed forces, except medical and religious personnel, that are engaged in combat action or in military operation preparatory to it; combatants must distinguish themselves from the civilian population.

The concept of combined arms integrates the application of several arms such as infantry, armour, aviation, artillery and engineers. Combined arms groups should be used within an air manoeuvre, ground manoeuvre forces wherever possible. Properly employed, combined arms groups provide a complementary range of capabilities of a well balanced force. They present few functional weaknesses for the enemy to exploit.

1. An order.
2. A field army formed by 2 or more corps.

Command is the authority invested in an individual for the direction, co-ordination, and control of military forces. Command is where the commander is.
Control is the process through which the commander, assisted by his staff, organises, directs and co-ordinates the activities of the forces allocated to him. Control is exercised by the designated headquarters.

C2W is the integrated use of all military capabilities including physical destruction, electronic warfare (EW), deception, psychological operations (PSYOPS) and operations security (OPSEC), supported by intelligence, to deny information, exploit, influence, degrade, confuse or destroy enemy C2 capabilities and to protect friendly C2 against such actions. In more simple terms, the objectives of C2W are the use of all military means to defeat the enemy's C2, while preserving your own.

Communication net connecting a command echelon or HQ with subordinate echelons or HQs for the purpose of command and control, e.g., the command net of an infantry battalion will include the battalion HQ and its company HQs.
A commander's tactical headquarters in war from where he exercises command and directs the operations.

An exercise of a HQ involving the commander and his staff, aimed at testing staff work and procedures and exercising the HQ in movement, development and the working of communication. Two levels of HQ can be exercised at the same time, e.g., Bde HQ and Bn HQ.

CCIRs are what the commander needs to know about:
a. His own forces and other friendly forces and the threat.
b. The battlefield environment in which he and the threat will be operating.
A historical record of the activities of all formation HQs and units, maintained in both peace and war.
A soldier in the special forces corps of amphibious infantry.

Commodity stores are categorised by need rather than type of store so that the management and distribution of resources can be targeted more efficiently. Categories of commodities are grouped into:
a. Operational items - Category O.
b. Training items - Category T.
c. Remainder - Category R.

A point which dispenses only one commodity and referred to by the type of commodity it provides. For example:
a. Ammunition Point (AP).
b. Ration Point (Rat P).
c. Petrol Point (PP).
A state achieved when groups of individuals, organisations or nations use common doctrine, procedures or equipment.

The passage of information in all forms through any of the following systems:
a. Physical (Courier/dispatch, hand/flag signalling).
b. Wireless.
c. Line.

CIS are the assembly of equipment, methods and procedures, and if necessary personnel, organised so as to accomplish specific information conveyance and processing functions. The effective employment and control of CIS resources are command responsibilities. They provide the means by which command and control is exercised.
An agency manned by signal personnel charged with the responsibility for the receipt, transmission and delivery of messages.

COMSEC is the way in which friendly force emissions are policed to ensure that should there be a security breach which will compromise operations, the appropriate remedial measures can be taken in time.

The rear part of the theatre of operations (behind but contiguous to the Combat Zone), which contains the lines of communication, establishments for supplies and evacuation, and other agencies required for the immediate support and maintenance of the forces in the Combat Zone.

The Comm Z is contiguous to the Combat Zone (see "Combat Zone"), and its extent will continue to change with the progress of operations.

The use of military forces on projects contributing to economic and social development useful to the local population at all levels, such as a field of education, training, public works, agriculture, transportation, communications, health and individual survival. It serves to improve the standing of the military forces and administration with the population. It is known as The Battle for Hearts and Minds.
Additional leave granted to service personnel to enable them attend to a serious personal or domestic matter.
Capability of two or more items or components of equipment or material to exist or function in the same system or environment without mutual interference.
A document containing lists of every item belonging to a piece of major equipment.
Packed rations, of assorted natures (e.g., biscuits, rice, beans, etc.), designed for field consumption. Most composite rations are already prepared, ready to eat.
Grouping of logistic units or installations for convenience of command and control.
Cover from view provided by a position, e.g. woods. It should not be confused with camouflage which is an artificial effort on men, vehicles and equipment to prevent being seen.

1. Type of artillery fire in which the fire of a number of guns is brought to bear on a particular target/targets. Concentrations are directed towards particular localities unlike barrages. It is the standard and quickest method of engaging a target. A concentration from a 105mm battery (Pack Howitzer) covers an area approximately 150 x 150 metres; a medium battery slightly more (about 250 x 250 metres).

2. Massing together of forces.
Area where troops taking part in an operation are concentrated, briefed and if possible rehearsed in their role.

This is the state of an equipment assessed at the time of an inspection. An equipment may be: S, X, Y, Z.
S - Serviceable.
X - Can be made serviceable by unit repairs.
Y - Can be made serviceable by field repairs.
Z - Can be made serviceable by intermediate or base repairs.

Confirmatory notes are notes similar in format and content to written operational orders. They should whenever possible be issued to recipients of oral orders at formation level. They provide an aide-memoire for those attending the orders and also valuable information for those not present such as staff officers at subordinate HQs. The discretion as to whether to issue confirmatory notes before or after delivery of the oral orders rests entirely with the commander.

Conflict is a situation in which violence is either manifest or threatened. It is a struggle or a clash between opposing forces or contending wishes. It does not always explicitly demand violence although the risk or threat of violence is implied.

Conflict prevention measures are usually conducted under Chapter IV of the UN Charter. They range from diplomatic initiatives to the deployment of forces intended to prevent disputes escalating into armed conflicts, or to prevent such conflict spreading to other regions.
Conflict termination is the termination of conflict by force, usually in conjunction with other coercive instruments of policy available to government.
In land warfare, a point on the terrain, easily identifiable, where two or more units are required to make contact.

The report of contact with the enemy, sent over the radio to the next higher commander. Visual contact with the enemy is enough to warrant a contact report. The sequence of reporting is as follows:
a. The time of contact.
b. Where the contact is; always given as a grid reference.
c. Details of the contact.
d. What the enemy is doing.
e. What you are doing about it.
To contain is to stop, hold, or surround the enemy forces or to cause the enemy to centre his activity on a given front and to prevent him withdrawing any part of his forces for use elsewhere.
Chemical contamination may be caused either directly by an attack, or indirectly by transfer from a contaminated surface.

Contamination control involves procedures to avoid, reduce, remove or render harmless, temporarily or permanently, chemical contamination for the purpose of maintaining or enhancing the efficient conduct of military operations.
Contingency planning is the process by which options including alternatives are built into a plan to anticipate opportunities or reverses.
System of supply whereby a vehicle moves continuously over a route being transferred from one driver to another driver at intermediate stages, normally at the Exchange Point (XP).
Difference in elevation between two adjacent Contour Lines.
A line on a map or chart connecting points of equal elevation.

A CRW terminology. It is an area not entirely free from the adversary in which conditions permit the civil administration and police to work effectively in co-operation with military forces. Although insurgent infiltration into controlled area is possible, the civil administration supported by military and/or para-military forces is capable of limiting insurgent activity, thereby separating the insurgent from the local population.

In COIN ops, Control measures are restrictive measures imposed upon a civil population and relating to such matters as movement, registration or the possession of food stocks or weapons. They are normally designed to separate the insurgents from the bulk of the population and deprive the insurgents of the resources they require.

An organization in an exercise with troops whose task it is to implement the exercise director's plan by the issue of exercise narratives, instructions, order of battle, briefs and forecasts of operations both before and during the exercise. The control organization will also be required to correlate the lessons learnt and prepare report on the exercise.
These are points set up by security forces to provide a military presence on the ground in a populated area where civil disturbances have taken or may take place.
The station in control of a radio net. See "Radio Station".

Vital items and stores which are in short supply either due to their expensive nature, e.g. air conditioners, weapons, etc. They are controlled and authorized for issue by the 'G' staff on a priority basis.

A carefully planned and executed offensive action where the various elements of a brigade group or division are employed in such a manner as to utilize their powers to the greatest advantage to the formation as a whole.

The Coordinating Conference is a type of backbrief which normally follows a set of orders. The purpose of the Coordinating Conference is to coordinate the commander's plan and to increase mutual understanding. It allows the commander to confirm that his subordinates understand his intent. There is no set format for a Coordinating Conference; it is very much dependent on the Commander's personal style.

A given line in a withdrawal (for an extrication) for which all troops are expected to cross by a given specific time, to allow friendly artillery commence engagement of the enemy with no fear of casualty to own troops.
A designated point at which, in all types of combat, adjacent units/formations must make contact for purposes of control and coordination.

The line beyond which conventional fire support means may fire at any one time, within the TAOR of the established HQ without additional coordination. The CFL is portrayed with a dashed line. The abbreviation 'CFL' is placed above the line and the effective DTG for use is placed below the line.

A combined police and military operation, based on good intelligence whereby a given area is cordoned and then searched for persons or to recover arms, ammunition, explosives, documents or any given items. Everything possible must be done to maintain secrecy and achieve surprise. The operation should be pre-planned in detail and rehearsed.
Core Functions of the Manoeuvrist Approach

a. At the operational level, 4 functions are derived from the Manoeuvrist Approach which are used mainly in the design and phasing of joint campaigns. Together they form a conceptual framework for the visualization and conduct of operations. These functions are:
(1) To shape the operational environment.
(2) To attack the adversary's cohesion.
(3) To protect the cohesion of own force.
(4) To exploit the situation by direct or indirect means, or a combination of both.

b. At the tactical level, where the focus is narrower, the core functions required to achieve success on the battlefield are: find, fix, strike and exploitation. These core functions should be conducted concurrently, or at least achieve smooth transition from one to another.
(1) Find. Finding spans locating, identifying, tracking and assessing the enemy. It is the effective use and coordination of all ISTAR assets in the commander's Intelligence Preparation of the Battlefield (IPB). Finding the enemy is implicit to the ability to fix and strike him successfully.
(2) Fix. To fix the enemy is to deny, distract, and deprive him of his goals and freedom of action in order to gain own freedom of action for successful operations. It is difficult to strike an enemy effectively if he is not fixed.
(3) Strike. To strike the enemy is to use the freedom of action "brought" by finding and fixing the enemy to manoeuvre - that is to get into a position in respect of the enemy from which you can hit him unexpectedly, or in superior force, at the point selected in order to defeat him.
(4) Exploitation. Exploitation is the seizure of opportunity in order to achieve a higher commander's objective, or fulfil some part of his intent, directly. Opportunities can occur at any time whilst finding, fixing or striking. A commander should constantly search for such opportunities and, when they occur, they should be pursued ruthlessly.

1. To neutralize the effect of.
2. To repel.
Air effort mounted to take out enemy aircraft both in the air and on the ground. One example is the Israeli air force action against the Egyptian air force during the 6-Day War of 1967.

C attk is an attack against an enemy attacking force for purposes of regaining lost ground, restore lost position or destroy en in order to regain control of an area which the en has secured. There are 2 types of C attk:
a. Immediate C attk. Launched spontaneously at level not lower than battalion group level to destroy local enemy penetration into battalion defences.
b. Deliberate C attk. Mounted as a deliberate attack, utilizing forces specifically earmarked for this task. Conducted usually at formation level using formation reserve.

Bombardment by artillery used to destroy or neutralize enemy guns, mortars, rockets and missile installations. A CB policy is usually laid down by a commander. It may be:
a. Active. Engage all hostile batteries.
b. Semi-Active. Engage only specified hostile batteries.
c. Silent. No engagement.
Operations and activities conducted by armed forces, paramilitary forces or non-military agencies against guerrillas.

Those military, para-military, political, economic, psychological and sociological activities undertaken by a government, independently or with assistance of friendly nations, to prevent or defeat subversive insurgency, and restore the authority of the central government.

A generic term to describe the operations which forces may have to undertake when maintaining and restoring law and order in support of an established government. These operations will have to counter threats posed by civil disturbances, terrorism and organised insurgency, irrespective of whether they are nationalist, communist or racially inspired, or directed from within or outside the state concerned.
That phase of intelligence activity devoted to destroying the effectiveness of inimical foreign intelligence and also provide protection against enemy's espionage, subversion and sabotage activities.
C pen is the use of reserve, uncommitted troops or depth groups to contain enemy penetration by blocking their advance.

A generic term to describe the operations which forces may have to undertake, when maintaining and restoring law and order in support of an established government, in order to counter the threats in an internal security or revolutionary war setting. These threats include civil disturbances, terrorism and organized insurgency, irrespective of whether these are nationalist, communist or racially inspired or directed from within or outside the threatened territory concerned.
C stroke is an attack movement to attack en in the flank, from ambush position, once he has penetrated the AOR.

That part of counter intelligence which is devoted to destroying the effectiveness of subversive activities through the detection, identification, exploitation, penetration, manipulation, deception and repression of individuals, groups or organisations conducting or capable of conducting such activities.
Offensive measures taken to prevent, deter and respond to terrorism.
Countermoves are operations undertaken in reaction to or in anticipation of a move by the enemy.
COA is what own forces or the threat might do in a particular situation.
The action by land, air, or sea forces to protect by offence, defence, or threat of either or both.

1. Any fire employed to keep the enemy's head down (thereby preventing aimed return fire) by fire support elements, while a manoeuvre element deploys.

2. The main reason for having an 'Arty Fire Plan'. It neutralizes enemy direct fire weapons during the movement of own troops from start line to objective. Usually preplanned.
Covering force is established by the highest tactical command to provide security for the main force.
The area forward of the forward edge of the battle area out to the forward positions initially assigned to the covering forces. It is here that the covering forces execute assigned tasks.
Covering troops are any detachment deployed by a commander at any level to provide protection for his main force. Depending on their tasks, they may be screens or guards (see "screens" or "guards").

Operations which are so planned and executed as to conceal the identity of the operators, or permit credible denial by the sponsor. They differ from clandestine operations in that emphasis is placed on concealment of the operation, i.e., disguised but not concealed.
The general line formed by joining the summits of the main ridge of a chain of mountains. False crest is the line along which lower steep slope changes to an upper gentle slope.

1. Negotiating an obstacle.
2. The methods of passing telephone lines, e.g., over a road (overhead or buried), on a river bed, etc.
The dispersal of a riotous assembly (a crowd) by the military, usually after the police have failed, based on the principle of minimum force.

In operational art, an operation reaches its culminating point when the current operation can just be maintained but not developed to any greater advantage. In the offence, the attacker reaches his culminating point when he can no longer sustain offensive operations and switches onto the defensive. In the defence, the defender reaches his culminating point when he can no longer maintain the defence and is compelled to disengage and withdraw or risk defeat.

A curfew is a restriction on movement of people within a given timing; it may be general and imposed over a wide but clearly defined area such as a city, district or region, or it may be restricted to a small area such as a town centre, a housing estate or a particular series of streets. The size of the area and the duration of time for which a curfew is imposed will depend on the reasons for it. Curfews may be needed to:
a. Assist the security forces in re-establishing control after rioting and serious disturbances have taken place, by restricting civil movement and allowing tempers to cool.
b. Prevent civil movement in a selected area while a search or the investigation of an incident is carried out.
c. Disrupt hostile groups by making movement of individuals difficult.
d. Allow the security forces greater freedom of operation.
Security procedure used to encode certain messages between formation levels of commands and above. Procedures for use are highly classified.

An expression of date and time together, in six figures followed by the Time Zone Suffix. The first pair figure indicates the day of the month, the second pair the hour, the third pair the minutes past the hour, e.g., 081755Z.
A planning figure representing the expected daily consumption of combat supplies of a force under specified conditions. A day of supply is not a fixed quantity, but is situation dependent.

Deceive/Deceptions are those measures designed to mislead the enemy by manipulation, distortion or falsification of evidence to induce him to react in a manner prejudicial to his interests. Deception forms an important component of Surprise and Security. To be effective, deception should be integrated from the highest level downwards, and will usually require the committal of significant forces or resources to convince the enemy.

In IPB, DPs are points in time and space, i.e., on the map, when the commander must make a decision if he is to influence the operation in a particular TAI. DPs, which are linked to particular TAIs, must be offset from the point where the action has to take place, in order to allow sufficient lead time for the action to be initiated.
DSO shows the TAIs and the corresponding DP to combine the G2 and G3 estimates in graphic form during the conduct of IPB.

1. In COIN ops, Deep Operations are designed to locate, disrupt and destroy hard core insurgents, with a view to reducing insurgent pressure and giving other operations a better chance of success. At the strategic level of conflict, Deep operations in COIN will tend to cover political, diplomatic and psychological operations, whereas, at the operational level of conflict, deep operations will generally be of a military nature.

2. See "Operational Framework".
Defeat can be defined as diminishing the effectiveness of the enemy to the extent that he is either unable to participate in combat or is unable to fulfil his intention.
The stated policy of the government of a nation regarding the defence of that nation's interest from both local and external threats.
Hold and deny to the enemy.

An area of ground organized for all-round defence where no indication of the extent of the area or the troops holding it is given. The levels are:
a. Defended Post. Det or sec.
b. Defended Locality. Pl or coy organized in depth.
c. Defended Area. Bn.
d. Defended Sector. Bde, div or corps.
e. Defended Zone. Army and above level; it has no formations on its flanks.

In CRW, Defended Villages are villages in controlled areas which have been organized for defence with a view to giving the inhabitants security from insurgent action, preventing subversive elements assisting the insurgent and encouraging the provision of information. Initially, defended villages may have to be manned by military forces, but in the long term the aim must be to train and organize home guards so that they and the police are able to take over the static defence from military forces.

Pre-arranged fire in the defence which can be brought down quickly on suspected or actual locations of enemy attacking forces. Types of the pre-arranged fire are:
a. DFs in Depth. Tasks in depth designed to neutralize and destroy enemy formations at the earliest possible moment. Generally, lies in a belt from about 1500 metres from the FEBA and beyond and are coordinated at brigade level.
b. Close DFs. Tasks designed to hit the enemy while he is in the FUP, start line or actually assaulting. Close DFs lie approximately 200 - 1500 metres from the FEBA.
c. Final Protective Fire (FPF). These are the most important close DFs where enemy threat is greatest or most probable, usually closest to the company localities. They should as much as possible coincide with natural or artificial obstacles, e.g., mines, streams, etc. Guns and mortars lay on their FPF when they are not engaging other targets to effect prompt response. A fire unit (field battery, medium, and mortar section) is allotted one FPF.
Protection from hostile ground observation and direct fire provided by an obstacle such as a hill, ridge or bank. It also implies achieving this protection through use of artificial obstacles.
A position which is protected naturally from observation and fire of flat trajectory weapons.

A defile is any natural or artificial feature which causes a body of troops to contract its normal front during its passage through it. A mountain pass is the most common type of natural defile; a bridge or a raised causeway through a marsh is an example of an artificial defile.

1. Process of withdrawal of military effect from military personnel leaving the service.

2. Process of making AFVs vehicles that have just crossed a water obstacle either by swimming or fording, ready for action. It involves lowering down screens (in screens down areas), and for forded tanks, removal of waterproofing equipment (in the dekitting area). Subsequently, post-flotation servicing and checks are carried out.
A selected report line which requires a delaying force to prevent the enemy from crossing that line until a specified time or the occurrence of an event.
The creation of a lane through a minefield or a clear route through a barrier or fortification, which is systematically planned and carried out.
The crossing of an inland water obstacle that requires extensive planning and detailed preparations.
Action taken to return to pre-mobilization status. See "Mobilization".

Demolition is the destruction of structure with explosives that is of strategic and tactical interest to the military during operation. See "preliminary demolition target" and "reserved demolition target".
Engineer party with technical responsibility for firing the demolition.

These are forms prepared by the authorised commander's G3 staff and contain orders and coordinating instructions for the demolition guard commander and the firing party commander. They also contain procedures for the delegation of authorised powers. These are:

a. AF W4012B. An army form containing orders to the Commander Demolition Firing Party to fire both reserved and preliminary demolitions. It also contains the order to change the State of Readiness.

b. AF W4012C. An army form containing orders to the Demolition Guard Commander of a reserved demolition.

Demolition Guard is a locally positioned force tasked to ensure demolition site is not captured by the enemy before it is successfully fired. The commander of the demolition guard is responsible for the operational command of all troops at the demolition site, including the demolition firing party. He is responsible for transmitting the order to fire to the demolition firing party.
To show by practical example, how a thing is done.
A show of force on a front where a decision is not sought or made. It is done with the aim of deceiving the enemy.
To prevent access by physical presence, blocking, disruption, dislocation and fire.

The expression by a commander delivering oral orders of how he intends to fight a battle throughout all its phases. It is in effect a short crisp summary of his chosen course. It is not specific as to particular tasks for formations or units as these are given in detail later.
To kill or so damage an enemy force that it is rendered useless.
A local civil telephone extension connected via a PUP to the civil system.
Line of sight fire, e.g., rifle, tank in primary role.

The support provided by a unit or formation not attached or under command/control of the supported unit or formation, but required to give a priority to the support required by that unit or formation.

Directives are defined as either 'a military communication in writing in which policy is established or a specific action is ordered', or 'any communication which initiates or governs action, conduct, or procedure'. A directive is employed at the higher levels of command to initiate activity and to give both general and specific guidance to subordinate commanders. Latitude is given to the addressee to use his discretion on implementing the directive. There are 3 types of directives: the Command Directive, Policy Directive and Planning Directives.

Discipline is the art of doing what is right and proper with or without supervision. It includes obedience to authority, conformity with regulations, adherence to positive societal norms and values and general good conduct in and out of uniform.
In a delay operation, when a large enemy force approaches to within a specified distance of a designated report line, then units may move from their delay positions.

To dislocate the enemy is to deny him the ability to bring his strengths to bear. For example, mounting a hasty attack on an enemy in his FUP prior to launching his attack would dislocate his plans and capability to retain the initiative.

A tactical task or obstacle effect (that integrates fire planning and obstacle effort) that breaks apart an enemy's formation and tempo, interrupts the enemy's timetable, causes premature commitment of forces, or forces him to attack piecemeal.

Disruption is by attacking the enemy selectively to break apart and throw into confusion the assets which are critical to the employment and coherence of his fighting power. For example, an attack on enemy artillery could severely disrupt the enemy's tactical capability.
The distribution of intelligence in a suitable form to those requiring it, in time for it to be used. It is the last stage of the Intelligence Cycle.
An individual who takes covert and overt action against a government.

A point located in the fwd BAA where stocks of C-sups are held on wheels by second line transport units from where they will be collected by unit echelons. The allocation of DPs is one per brigade. Depending on the tactical situation, terrain and routes, second line transport may distribute C-sups direct to unit locations, especially fwd movement of arty ammunition. Distribution points usually carry no stock items; items drawn are issued completely as soon as possible.
The act of drawing the attention and forces of an enemy from the point of the principal operation; an attack, or alarm, or feint which diverts attention.

Administrative area generally located toward the rear of the divisional area which contains unit B echelons and those brigade logistic elements which are not located in the forward BAAs and divisional logistic units. The DAA is controlled by rear divisional HQ which may be located in or adjacent to it. The officer responsible for it is nominated by the divisional commander but is usually the G4 staffs. Only 2-3 days of supplies are normally held.
A DSG will be established to coordinate and control CSS to the Division. It will be located at the DAA.

In IPB, a doctrinal overlay shows what the friendly forces and the threat would probably do on a "flat playing field" based on their doctrine with no terrain constraints. It is produced on clear unmarked overlays without showing the "No Go and Slow Go" areas.
Military doctrine is fundamental principles by which military forces guide their action in support of objective. It is authoritative but requires judgment in application.

Document security entails all documents to be protected in accordance with their classification. Distribution of classified documents should be limited to those with a need to know, and delivery means assessed for risk.
A specified area onto which airborne troops, equipment or supplies are airdropped.
Another name for Phoney Minefield. See "Minefield".
A temporary storage area, usually in the open, for bombs, ammunition, equipment or supplies.
Dumping is the placing of stocks on the ground, additional to reserve stocks normally carried on wheels.
A dune is a hill or ridge of sand formed by the wind.

Terminology employed in mechanized operations. Means the distance between AFVs in which the dust cloud of a leading AFV does not affect the crew of the following AFV(s). Dust distance will vary according to the nature of country.
The day on which an exercise commences.

The various types of echelon in a Battalion Group are sub-divided as follows:

F Echelon
F Echelon comprises all fighting elements of the battalion including all the headquarters and sub-unit logistic assets such as ambulances and fitter sections.

A1 Echelon
A1 Echelon is composed of the personnel and vehicles required to provide an immediate or emergency resupply of fuel and ammunition for the battalion at any stage of operations. It may also include the Regimental Aid Post (RAP), if not grouped with F Echelon. It will normally operate centrally under battalion control, but may be placed under sub-unit command when the battalion is operating on a wide frontage.

A2 Echelon
