Although A2 Echelon will frequently be under brigade command for movement and local defence and will be located with the Brigade Support Group (BSG), it will be under the logistics command of the battalion. It consists of:
(1) The remainder of the battalion's combat supply transport and stocks.
(2) Technical stores.
(3) Repair and recovery resources to augment sub-unit fitter sections.

B Echelon
B Echelon consists of the Quartermaster's Department, the Regimental Administration Office and any other elements left out of battle, including battle casualty replacements. It will be located with the Brigade or Divisional Support Groups.
Confirmed maximum range up to which destructive power is guaranteed for the weapons concerned.
The ability of a target audience to respond to a psychological objective. (Used in a psy ops context.)
The deliberate prohibition of electronic radiations, normally applied for a stated period, to specific equipments or frequency bands.

EW is the military action involving the use of electromagnetic energy to determine, exploit, reduce or prevent hostile use of the electromagnetic spectrum and action to retain its effective use by friendly forces. The components of EW are: EW = ESM (passive offensive) + ECM (active offensive) + EPM (defensive).

a. Electronic Warfare Support Measures (ESM). ESM is the principal information gathering and target identification activity of EW. It finds and exploits enemy transmissions and the location of emitters. This applies to both communications and non-communications (radars, lasers, etc.) transmissions.

b. Electronic Counter Measures (ECM). ECM is the prevention of the enemy's use of the electromagnetic spectrum by Electronic Jamming and the use of other forms of Electronic Attack to influence his activities. It is the offensive and active arm of EW and is used to fix and to strike at the enemy.

c. Electronic Protective Measures (EPM). EPM is the protection of friendly communications and non-communications systems against the enemy's attempts to find, fix and strike at them.

That part of an amphibious force that assaults or, in the case of minor operations, goes ashore. In a major operation, it should consist of an all arms group and it can expect fire support and logistic support from ships, aircraft and helicopters. The size and grouping of the embarked force will depend on the operation and the resources available.
EMCON provides selective and controlled use of electro-magnetic, acoustic or other emitters, to optimise command and control while minimizing detection and exploitation of an enemy's sensors.
A well-fortified gun position or machine gun nest.
Documents which are complete in themselves and sent with a covering document.
The clearing of opposition either by the Vanguard or Advance Guard.

Forcing a passage across a water obstacle lightly held by the enemy, off the line of march. Momentum of the advance is thus maintained. Speedy recce, good engineer intelligence and correct grouping of forces are essential for success. Also known as "hasty crossing".
End State is that state of affairs which needs to be achieved at the end of a campaign either to terminate the conflict or resolve it on favourable terms.
In air defence, a fire control order used to direct or authorise units and/or weapon systems to fire on a designated target.

An offensive action at formation and above level in which the main attack strikes the enemy from the rear. Essentially involves an outflanking movement which passes round or through the enemy positions to cut off his withdrawal routes, line of maintenance and destroy him. Alternatively, the movement may be two-pronged, one element to block the enemy from the front. Envelopment may be single or double:

a. Single. Manoeuvre against one flank or around one flank against the rear of the initial disposition of the enemy.

b. Double. Otherwise called encirclement. This is envelopment from both flanks simultaneously.
All non-expendable items needed to outfit or equip an individual or organisation.

A location usually in or near the forward BAA where equipment casualties from units and LADs are collected before back loading by second line recovery resources. It is often convenient to locate it near the FRG (Forward Repair Group).
Any person who, after physical capture by the enemy, successfully escapes into an area under own, friendly or neutral control.
Escarpment is an extended line of cliffs. That is, ground with sheer drop on one side.
A combatant unit(s) assigned to accompany and protect another force or convoy.

That relationship existing in a unit, formation or corps borne out of pride and confidence by all ranks belonging to that unit, formation or corps to the extent that the average soldier believes himself fortunate to belong to a particular unit and feels rather sorry for those soldiers who do not belong. Esprit-de-corps considerably enhances discipline. This is because the individual is even more ready to sacrifice his own interests for the common good.
Covert means of obtaining information of the enemy or potential enemy including his future strategic plans.

An estimate process is a logical process of reasoning by which a commander considers all circumstances affecting the military situation and arrives at a decision on the course of action (COA) to be adopted to accomplish his mission.

There are three types of Estimate Process:
a. Operational Estimate
The Operational Estimate is designed for a Joint Task Force Commander (JTFC) at the operational level to develop a campaign plan and subsequently modify operation orders and directives.
The estimate must be command-led, as it supports the JTFC's decision-making process. All other estimates, regardless of command level, should contribute to the Operational Estimate.

b. Tactical Estimate
The Tactical Estimate provides a planning process for formation headquarters conducting complex planning, with sufficient time available, within the context of an established campaign plan.
It is used where campaign planning concepts have already been determined at the operational level by the Joint Force Headquarters (JFHQ). Like the Joint Operational Estimate, the Tactical Estimate seeks to develop a winning concept through analysis guided by the JTFC's direction.

c. Combat Estimate
The Combat Estimate is also known as the 7-Questions Combat Estimate. It is primarily used at the lower tactical levels for decision-making during battles and engagements, particularly when time is limited.
It enables commanders at lower levels of command to apply their intuition, experience and training, especially during the heat of action, to streamline decision-making and produce a practical and workable plan.
The tidal mouth of a river. A section of a river meeting the sea.
The movement of human and equipment casualties out of the area of operations.

An event overlay is derived from the situation overlay; it shows graphically the Named Area of Interest (NAI) where key tactical events are likely to take place. The identification of these NAIs will prompt the tasking of RISTA to maintain surveillance over these areas.

1. The replacement of clothing and stores items that are either damaged or have outlived their usefulness, e.g., military uniforms.

2. Telephone exchange.

A point deployed by the highest HQ in an operation to shorten the turnaround where the replenishment park is too far to the rear for second line transport to get there and back within twenty-four hours.

An exempt call is defined as a call to those stations normally designated by a collective or all stations call, less certain specifically exempted stations. It is used when a calling station wishes to call the majority, but not all of the stations associated with a collective or all stations call. Exempt calls can simplify calls and prevent unnecessary replies.
A military manoeuvre or simulated wartime operation involving planning, preparation and execution. It is carried out for the purpose of training and evaluation.

1. An offensive operation that usually follows a successful attack and is designed to disorganise the enemy in depth. See "Core Functions of the Manoeuvrist Approach".

2. Taking full advantage of success in battle and following up initial gains.

3. Taking full advantage of any information that has come to hand for tactical or strategic purposes.
All ammunition containing explosives, nuclear, biological and chemical agents including improvised explosive devices and all similar or related items or components that are explosive in nature.
The detection, identification, field evaluation, rendering safe, recovery and final disposal of unexploded explosive ordnance.
A form of positional defence employed on a wide front. It is characterized by large gaps, limited mutual support, greater depth of position and a strong reserve.
In a military operation, extraction is the urgent removal of an individual or a group of individuals or materiel from a threat.
The time designated for the start of FLOT aviation operations.
A facility for transmitting a document, e.g., map, table or diagram, over a voice circuit.

1. To dismiss a soldier(s) from a superior officer's/NCO's imm presence.

2. Radioactive materials deposited on the surface of the earth following the explosion of nuclear weapons, not only in the immediate vicinity of the explosion but over any region of the globe.

That degree of dominance in the air battle of one force over another, which permits the conduct of operations by the former and its related land, sea and air forces at a given time and place, without prohibitive interference by the opposing air force.
The purpose of a feint attack is to distract the action of an enemy force by seeking contact with it.

Medical unit that provides second line medical cover to units; it is allocated on a scale of one per brigade. It is fully mobile on organic transport and carries sufficient tentages to enable it work in the field when suitable buildings are not available. In war, a field ambulance normally establishes one dressing station, the Main Dressing Station (MDS), where casualties receive treatment, are documented and prepared for future evacuation. The MDS in this case is normally sited in the fwd BAA. Sometimes, however, in order to meet operational exigencies, a field ambulance can, as an exception, provide two dressing stations: the MDS and the Advance Dressing Station (ADS). This is to cover long communication lines characteristic of the Advance and Withdrawal operations of war. In this case, it is normal for the ADS to be located in the fwd BAA and the MDS in the BAA.
Branch of artillery that is concerned with finding and engaging ground targets with indirect fire support of infantry and armour. Provides 'Close Support' and General Support.

The basic field training given to an individual soldier to enable him take his proper place in the military team under operational conditions. It includes the basic fundamentals of fire and movement, observation, judging distance, seeing without being seen and hearing without being heard, and camouflage and concealment. It also includes how to make the best possible use of cover and how to move with weapons and equipment.
An area in which it will be possible to fire effectively from a given position and which is related to a particular weapon.
Postal facility established in the Combat Zone.

Field signals are alternative means of passing orders and controlling troops by the use of hands, limbs, weapons and whistle when voice control is not possible owing to battle noises, need for silence and intervening distances being too much for effective voice control.
Aircraft used for close air support mission.

Fighting power defines an army's ability to fight. It is expressed in qualitative terms, reflecting the suitability for employment in a particular environment of operations. Fighting power is made up of 3 components: conceptual, physical and moral components.

a. Conceptual Components. This can be described as the thought process behind the ability to fight. It is made up of Principles of War, military doctrine and development.

b. The Moral Component. The moral component concerns with the ability to get people to fight. It will involve motivation, leadership and management.

c. The Physical Component. The physical component is the means to fight. It is the equivalent of the term 'combat power' (see "combat power"). Physical component includes the following elements: manpower, equipment, logistics/sustainability, training and readiness.

Area close to the objective where assaulting troops, if not already so deployed, adopt their formation for the final assault. It may not be possible to lay down the precise positions at orders and is more likely to be indicated by radio or verbally during the attack.
See "Core Functions of the Manoeuvrist Approach".

The principle of having one 'leg' on the ground providing security and providing fire or being ready to fire, while the other 'leg' moves (i.e., one leg up, one down). The idea is to ensure a proper balance and close coordination of fire power (including air support) with the tactical mobility of the combat arms for the successful execution of a ground battle.

FCA is an area subject to specific restraints into which fire support in excess of those restraints (weight of fire, types of ammo, etc.) will not be delivered without the prior approval of the authority establishing the restraint.
'Fire for effect' means produce the full weight of fire requested in initial orders. This term is applicable to indirect fire and is issued after satisfactory ranging.

1. Initial warning order when requesting for fire, transmitted over the radio by an observer (supported arm, e.g., Infantry) to an OP officer (Arty officer to whom fire request is made).

2. Specific assignment given to a fire unit as part of a definite plan.
Plan involving the dovetailing of available supporting fire resources (including tank fire) to achieve the best possible utilization of the weapons in support of a unit or formation.

A cell where detailed planning, control and coordination of fire support is carried out at battalion group level. The FSC is supervised by the BC of the Direct Support battery who advises the battalion group commander on all fire support matters. The BC is assisted by the support company commander or mortar platoon commander. The FSC is also responsible for air safety within the battalion group air space and might include a forward air controller (FAC).

A line established by the appropriate ground commander to ensure coordination of fire not under his control but which may affect current tactical operations. The FSCL is used to coordinate fire of air, ground or sea weapon systems using any type of ammunition against surface targets.
Measure taken to coordinate the fire of disparate fire units and to minimise fratricide.
Fire trench is that part of a battle trench from which the enemy may be observed and engaged.

The minimum number of weapons that can be employed on any one serial of a fire plan. Below this level, fire is considered largely ineffective. A fire unit may be:
a. One field battery (but four guns can be used for a smoke serial and only two for illumination).
b. A troop of a medium battery (because of their heavier shells).
c. A platoon of tanks.
d. Two fighter ground attack (FGA) aircraft.

The quantity of C sups which is normally held by a unit on first line (i.e., organic) transport. It is calculated to sustain that unit in operations for a specific length of time without re-supply. It is controlled by the unit commander. If unit transport cannot carry the first line scale, the balance is either dumped in or near the unit's location or carried by second line transport.
Vehicle made according to specifications to carry radios and operate as vehicular stations, e.g., FFR Land Rover.
See "Core Functions of the Manoeuvrist Approach".
A tactical obstacle effect that integrates fire planning and obstacle effort to slow down an attacker within a specified area, normally an engagement area.

A fixed line is a given line and point of aim on which a weapon is capable of firing from during mist, darkness or under poor visibility. It is not necessary for the target to be visible when a weapon is set on fixed line as the weapon is so sited that its fire is effective on a selected area of ground. Fire on fixed line is opened on a pre-arranged signal order.

A foot march by soldiers (sometimes displaying military hardware including AFVs) in a civilian environment either to sell the military profession to civilians or in a CRW environment to serve as a deterrent to potential troublemakers.
A security element operating to the flank of a moving or stationary force to protect it from enemy ground observation, direct fire, and surprise attack.
The means by which enemy interference by fire or assault onto the flanks of own force(s) is dealt with.
Direct fire weapons with line of sight aiming, e.g., 107mm Anti-Tank gun, etc.
This is a table (Relative Strength Table) comparing the strength of friendly and threat forces, at agreed intervals, to determine whether or not a force has achieved desired norms.
Foreshore is that portion of the shore between high and low watermarks.

Fording is the movement of a vehicle on the bed of a water obstacle. A certain amount of preparation is usually carried out on the vehicle, depending on the depth of the water. For tanks and AFVs, fording may be:
a. Shallow. No preparation is required for the vehicle. Top of the engine compartment and exhaust opening remain outside the water.
b. Medium. Water level is up to turret ring. Preliminary preparations like sealing the top of the engine compartment and fitting special one-way valves on the exhaust are required. The driver will have to be directed by the tank commander.
c. Deep. Otherwise called immersed fording or snorkelling. The tank is completely submerged. Air for intake by the engine and breathing by crew is introduced by snorkel apparatus. The driver maintains direction by gyrocompass or by guidance via the radio, from outside.
Brigade, division and corps are all referred to individually as formation.
The last position occupied by the assault echelon before crossing the start line/line of departure.
An officer, warrant officer or senior NCO who, from a forward ground or air position, directs the action of combat aircraft engaged in offensive close air support of land force.

Area which contains battalion A2 echelons and in addition may contain elements of logistic units, some of which would be under divisional control, which must be deployed in the brigade area in order to operate efficiently, e.g., DP. All units in the fwd BAA are controlled by the brigade HQ.

FEBA is the foremost limit of area where ground combat troops are deployed, excluding areas which the covering troops/screening forces are operating, designated to coordinate fire sp and positioning of forces or the manoeuvre of units.
FLOT is the line which indicates the most fwd positions of friendly forces in any kind of military operations at a specific time.

A secure base, port or airfield, from which an operation may be launched. It is normally, but not necessarily, external to the theatre of operations and may be an essential stepping-stone into that theatre.
The Arty Officer in an OP, when the OP is mobile, e.g., in an advance. A field battery produces 3 FOOs.

An area providing a semi-permanent firm base from which offensive action against the insurgents can be developed. It should be established at a seat of local government as a formation base, usually at brigade level, and will normally have a Tactical Transport (Medium range or short range) airfield, capable of quick development.

An operation in which a force advances or attacks through another force which is in contact with the enemy. The force in contact remains in place and must provide the advancing force with as much assistance as possible including tactical and logistical support. A forward passage of lines will be used when:
a. An attack is to be continued with fresh or more suitable forces.
b. The force to be relieved is closely engaged with the enemy.
c. The advancing force has to take possession of suitable terrain in order to continue the battle.

An area under cover in the vicinity of an objective to which tanks go when released from dominating the objective, and from which they are immediately available to return to fire positions or to support counterattacks.

A repair organization provided by an armoured or infantry workshop to carry out priority second line repairs in forward units. The FRG is based on forward repair teams (FRT) - four FRTs for infantry workshops, considerably more for armoured workshops. The FRG is formed by adding elements from the MT platoon and the stores section NAOC to the FRTs provided by the repair company.
A workshop repair section of up to 50 men formed by base workshop and deployed usually to carry out unit and field repairs in an emergency.

Repair elements of the FRG that carry out priority tasks like replacement of major assemblies in forward units locations. Each FRT consists of up to four tradesmen mounted in a vehicle capable of lifting major assemblies up to three tonnes for an armoured workshop and up to one tonne for an Infantry workshop.

The four fundamental questions that must be addressed when assessing logistic requirements are the starting point of all Combat Service Support (CSS) planning. They are:

Destination, Demand, Distance and Duration (4Ds).
a. Destination
Destination establishes the overall environment in which an operation will take place. It determines the conditions affecting equipment wear and tear, the physiological demands on troops and the strategic Lines of Communication (L of C).
b. Demand
Demand encompasses the rate of consumption and usage of materiel. It stems directly from the commander's intent and the nature of the operation.
c. Distance
Distance requires consideration of both the strategic Lines of Communication and those within the theatre of operations, before, during and after the operation.

The length, capacity and topography of the Lines of Communication determine the size, shape, structure and balance of the CSS resources required.
d. Duration
The duration of an operation, together with the rate of demand, determines the overall volume of materiel required and the scale of the logistic problem.

It also determines endurance requirements, the need to rotate or replace personnel and equipment, and medical holding policies.

A FragO may be written, graphical/schematic, oral or a combination of these methods. It is used to supplement or amend an operation order. It should follow the same paragraph format as the order which it is to supplement or amend. Where there is "no change" to a paragraph it must be annotated as such.
Fratricide is the unintentional killing or wounding of friendly personnel by fire.
An offensive manoeuvre in which the main effort is directed against the front of the enemy force(s).
This is combat order (see "Combat Order") plus rucksack and is a load which will be required for an operation of up to two weeks duration without resupply except for ammunition, rations and water.
A command based on military functions rather than geographic areas.
The authority vested in a commander of one of the Services, a specialist agency or MOD branch acting on behalf of a Service Board.

Functions in Combat are practical conceptual tools deduced from the Principles of War and required to implement the Manoeuvrist Approach to operations. The 6 principal functions in combat are:

a. Information and Intelligence. Accurate and timely intelligence is fundamental to the success of all operations. Much of this information is derived from Reconnaissance, Intelligence, Surveillance and Target Acquisition (RISTA).

b. Manoeuvre. To manoeuvre is to seek to get into a position of advantage in respect of the enemy, from which force can be threatened or applied.

c. Firepower. Firepower destroys, neutralises and suppresses; it is essential in defeating an enemy's ability to fight.

d. Protection. Protection preserves the fighting potential of a force so that it can be applied at a decisive time and place.

e. Combat Service Support (CSS). CSS sustains the force. It is the support provided to combat forces, primarily in the fields of personnel and logistics.

f. Command. Command is the exercise of authority and direction by a designated commander for the planning, direction, coordination and control of a military force.
The day and/or time on which an order (normally national) is given to deploy a unit.

Military gamble is an operation which can lead either to victory or the complete destruction of one's force. It is an operation of great risk; for instance, when defeat is imminent and gaining time is pointless, the only chance left is a "gamble".

Five and ten tonne trucks required to move men and materials from the rear areas into the Combat Zone. It is from these transport resources that ST companies will move combat supplies forward from RP to XP and further to the DP.

That support which is given to the supported force as a whole and not to any particular sub-division thereof. Often used to refer to artillery which is used to influence the corps or divisional battle and normally tasked for counter battery and other depth targets. There is no guarantee of fire to the manoeuvre arm.

Gen Sp Rft artillery has the mission of supporting the forces as a whole and, on a secondary basis, of providing reinforcing fire for another artillery unit. Artillery allocated in this role has two priorities: the first is to the Comd Arty and the second is to the supported formation. It provides therefore a certain degree of guaranteed fire though it is likely to have an ammunition caveat.
An unrestricted conflict between major powers. This might include widespread use of nuclear, chemical and possibly biological weapons.
Those regulations governing the treatment and handling of prisoners of war (POWs). POWs are expected to be treated firmly, fairly and humanely.
The systematic killing of all the people from a national, ethnic, or religious group, or an attempt to do this.

In conducting IPB, "Go" areas are grounds which are open and suitable for manoeuvre. It must be assessed according to the type of force; for example, what is "Go" to the dismounted forces might not be "Go" to the armour or mounted forces.
A gorge is a deep narrow valley which is rugged and usually rocky.
Grid is a system of squares formed by lines, which represent progressive distances EAST and NORTH of a fixed point.
The direction of an object from a point, expressed as an angle (degree or mil) measured clockwise with reference to grid north.
GTI is the ground the possession of which by the en will seriously interfere with the successful def of the position.

There are three types of ground manoeuvre forces: Heavy, Medium and Light Forces. They usually operate in combination to achieve the desired operational effect.

a. Heavy Forces
Heavy forces consist primarily of heavy armoured fighting vehicles. They utilise automotive power to deliver considerable firepower, protection and battlefield mobility.
However, their employment may be restricted by complex terrain. Their operational and strategic mobility are also constrained by their weight and logistic requirements. Despite these limitations, they remain a major component of many land forces.

b. Medium Forces
Medium forces consist primarily of light armoured vehicles. They are more strategically and operationally deployable than heavy forces and may constitute some of the first elements to deploy into a theatre of operations.

c. Light Forces
Light forces consist primarily of foot infantry troops. They possess significant strategic mobility because they can be transported by aircraft to almost any theatre of operations.
They may also be the only forces capable of operating effectively in complex terrain. However, their firepower is limited compared to heavy and medium forces, and they are more vulnerable.
Providing light forces with additional mobility or firepower through the use of Armoured Personnel Carriers (APCs) gives them some characteristics of medium forces. However, this may reduce their strategic mobility and operational utility.

The plan to coordinate the employment of patrols, Ops, FOO and MFC zones of observations, aerial recce and surveillance devices. This is to enable the commander watch the battlefield at all times and gather combat intelligence in time for him to react and retain the initiative.
The point on the ground surface vertically beneath or above which a nuclear weapon has exploded. Maximum damage from the nuclear explosion will be recorded on the Ground Zero.
Combined arms training from company group level.
Allotment of arms and services under one commander for a task.

This is the division of a battlegroup into functional groups to achieve effective concurrent activity prior to an operation. The composition of each group will vary according to the task, as explained below:
a. Reconnaissance Group (R Group). The R Group is responsible for reconnaissance and planning. The group includes those necessary to give the appropriate advice, a security element and communications.
b. Orders Group (O Group). The O Group receives orders and contains all those with a part to play in the forthcoming operation. From these orders, recipients extract the appropriate information and issue their own orders. may undertake preliminary moves, whilst orders are being written and given.
c. Main Body. The main body prepares for the operation and may undertake preliminary moves, whilst orders are being written and given.
d. Harbour and Rear Recce Parties. If the main body has to move forward to a concentration or assembly area, a harbour party will be despatched ahead of the main body. Its tasks will be to recce and lay out the new area and then to guide the main body, as they arrive, to their positions. If it is necessary for a battlegroup to withdraw, it is usual to despatch a rear recce group. This group combines a tactical reconnaissance function with that of the normal harbour party in the event of having to fight from this position upon their arrival.
Guards are covering troops deployed to delay the en for a specified period, additional to observation and report on en movement.
Tank designated for 'sentry' tasks in a combat team leaguer. The tank remains fully manned for the period it is so designated.

Military or para-military operations conducted in enemy held or hostile territory by irregular, predominantly indigenous force. Guerrilla warfare will be the main preoccupation of security forces in counter insurgency.

Weapons in which the projectiles are remotely guided by an external mechanism onto a target after firing. In some cases, the weapons are fed with relevant data and the projectiles take over the guidance automatically and home on to their targets.

a. The specific time at which an operation or exercise commences or is due to commence. It is also the time at which the Line of Departure (LD) is crossed by the leading elements in an attack.
b. In amphibious operations, the time at which the first waterborne wave of an amphibious assault lands on the beach.
Hachuring is a conventional method of representing hill features by short disconnected lines drawn directly down the slope in the direction of the flow of water on the slopes.
A control feature, preferably following easily defined terrain features, at which responsibility for the conduct of combat operations is passed from one force to another.

An area well out of contact where a force lies up for any length of time for administrative convenience (e.g., refit, rest, reorganization and maintenance). Protection and concealment will be maintained.

A party formed when required for a specific task, e.g., recce and planning of a new harbour area (See "Grouping System"). On completion of the task, members rejoin their normal echelons. At battalion level, it will be commanded by the 2IC and will include representatives of the company groups and specialist subunits.
In land operations, an attack in which preparation time is traded for speed in order to exploit an opportunity.
The rapid creation of a route through a minefield, barrier or fortification by any expedient method.
The crossing of an inland water obstacle using the crossing means at hand or those readily available and made without pausing for elaborate preparations.

A defence normally organised while in contact with the enemy or when contact is imminent and time available for the organisation is limited. It is characterised by improvement of the natural defensive strength of the terrain by utilisation of foxholes, emplacements, and obstacles.

The word headquarters is often used as a generic term for the grouping of the staff, its associated CIS and a structure which provides a working environment. There are 6 types of headquarters and they are described below:
a. Main Headquarters (Main). As the name implies this is the central controlling headquarters (at any level) where all the staff functions of that headquarters are coordinated and where the command and control of all subordinate units is focussed. The headquarters itself is normally commanded by the COS who decides on its composition, organisation, siting and tactical deployment.
b. Forward Headquarters (Fwd HQ). This is usually an advance or detached element of the HQ, perhaps deployed early into theatre, with a skeleton communications infrastructure and very limited protection. It would typically be mounted in soft-skinned vehicles. Fwd HQ lacks the resources to support command in battle.
c. Tactical Headquarters (Tac HQ). All field headquarters require to be tactical. If a headquarters has become too large and unwieldy, then its structure should be pruned. Tac HQ refers to a small HQ (Comd and principal Arms Advisers as appropriate) complete with sufficient mobility, protection and communications to command the battle for limited periods away from Main.
d. Alternate Headquarters (Alt HQ). Alternate headquarters provide continuity of command when a headquarters either needs to be moved or is put out of action.
e. Step-Up Headquarters (Step-Up). If fewer vehicles, manpower and CIS are available, a Step-Up headquarters may replicate only key functions and be capable of holding control for only limited periods while a Main headquarters moves and while men and vehicles are transferred from the previous Main headquarters location.
f. Rear Headquarters (Rear). The principal location for the designated commander of any rear operations including combat service support activity.

Hide is a concealed position in which a force waits before operation or before moving into battle position. A subunit hide should provide:
a. Overhead protection (OHP) and concealment against en action and observation.
b. All-round defence.
c. Dispersion.
d. Easy access and breakout.
HPTs are those targets/assets whose acquisition and successful attack will contribute substantially to the success of the friendly commander's mission.
A HPTL is a list of HPTs in priority.
HVTs are those targets/assets which the enemy commander requires for the successful completion of his mission and are, therefore, of high value to him.

Hold is applicable to both defence and attack:
a. In defence. To hold is to maintain or retain possession of a position or an area by force.
b. In an attack. Holding Attack is to exert sufficient pressure to hold the enemy in position to deceive him as to where the main attack is coming from. This is to prevent movement, re-disposition of enemy forces and also to prevent him from reinforcing his elements and/or to cause him to commit reserves prematurely at an indecisive location.

Homing is a process whereby an aircraft, using a homing facility, can locate and home on to any VHF/FM station within range by receiving voice transmissions or carrier waves transmitted by the ground station for short periods. Homing facilities are used when a pilot has difficulty locating a ground station. Homing indications are only displayed while the ground station is transmitting.
A Homer is a radio navigation facility or equipment that enables an aircraft to locate and navigate towards a ground radio station by detecting its VHF/FM transmissions.
The distance measured on the map between adjacent contours or between two points.

Civil and military assistance rendered in peace and war by a host nation to allied forces which are located on or in transit through the host nation's territory. The basis of such assistance is commitments arising from bilateral or multilateral agreements concluded between the host nation and the nation(s) having forces operating on the host nation's territory.
A gun with a high angle (45° - 80°) capability, giving it the same ability as mortars in engaging targets on reverse slopes, etc.
Normal tank position for direct fire; only the turret is visible to the enemy.
A system using electromagnetic transmissions to which equipment carried by friendly forces automatically responds, for example by emitting pulses, thereby distinguishing themselves from enemy forces.
The use of white light at any stage of a night attack.

II is a passive device used to make objects visible in darkness. The II principle basically involves the use of ambient light to intensify the image of the objects electronically, thereby making the objects visible.

Air support to meet specific requests which arise during the course of a battle, and which by their nature cannot be planned in advance as opposed to pre-planned air support for which notification is made in advance (normally forty-eight hours in advance).
Ground that is highly desirable rather than essential to hold.

An imprest account is the account maintained in a command into which all public funds released to the command to meet expenditure under the approved Army allocation is paid. The purpose of imprest account is to record receipts and subsequent expenditure of the funds into it.

Implies the fire or locating effort of the arty unit is normally guaranteed and arty liaison is provided at every level of command (e.g., FOO at Coy level, BC at Bn-level, etc.). Thus an arty unit or subunit can only be placed in direct support of one battalion group or formation. Arty in direct support provides:
a. Advice and communication to the supported arm.
b. Observation (if applicable) to the front and flanks.
c. Guaranteed fire support from its guns.
An expression used to denote the task of providing artillery supporting fire to a formation or unit. Liaison and observation are not normally provided.

All forms of training of the soldier, NCO, warrant officer and officer as an individual to enable each take his proper place and play his part adequately in his arm or service. Some of the aspects of individual training in the infantry for example include physical fitness training, shooting and weapon handling, communication skills, helicopter drills, preparation of fire and shelter trenches and overhead protection, night training, AFV and aircraft recognition, field craft, general knowledge, etc. Some of these aspects are common to all arms and services.
A methodical process of interrogation, discussion, propaganda and harassment designed to alter people's concepts and convictions and to condition them to accepting a new ideology or thinking.
The Infantry mission is 'to close with and engage the enemy in concert with other arms, through fire and manoeuvre in all operational theatres and environments, in order to bring about his defeat'.
Modified APC that not only carries the infantry to the battlefield, but also into it. The main modification is on increased armament, thereby giving the infantry more teeth.
Telephone mounted at the rear of the hull of a tank to facilitate infantry men from outside the tank speaking with individual tank commanders within. Not all tanks carry infantry telephones.
A technique and process in which a force moves as individuals or small groups over, through or around enemy positions without detection.

Unprocessed or 'raw' data which may either be used simply to inform about some matter or, which can be subjected to an analytical process, in order to assess a capability or predict what the outcome of an event may be.
INFOSEC is the security of Information Systems (IS), including hardware, software and bearer systems. Particular attention should be paid to IS using commercial bearer systems, such as the Internet.
A person who provides information to a collection agency. See "Sources and Agencies".
A member of an organisation who passes information to the opponents of the organization.

Active night fighting device which enables the user to see in darkness, also called red light. The system depends upon emitting an IR beam which is invisible to the naked eye but when viewed through special IR viewing device appears as light. It can be detected by an enemy with an IR capability.

IRLS is a sensor employed by reconnaissance aircraft to detect natural infrared radiation on the ground. It is of particular value in the jungle because of its ability to penetrate natural cover although water vapour in the atmosphere tends to degrade the resolution obtained.
Any logistic or administrative base. This definition also includes POW camps.

An instruction is used to regulate military activity; it complements directives or orders. Examples are:
a. Standing Instructions. Standing Instructions are issued typically to set out organisational responsibilities and to govern routine administrative procedures and actions.
b. Periodic Instructions. Periodic Instructions cater for any specific actions required of a non-routine nature.
c. Formal Instructions. Formal Instructions carry authority equivalent to that of directives or orders.

A form of rebellion in which a dissident faction that has the support or acceptance of a substantial part of the population instigates the commission of widespread acts of civil disobedience, sabotage and terrorism, and wages guerrilla warfare in order to overthrow a government. A state of insurgency implies that the insurgents have control of sizeable areas of the country and that it will almost inevitably be part of a revolutionary war on the communist pattern.

Insurgent is a term that can be used in place of any of these following terms when applicable; these are: guerrilla, revolutionary, terrorist, dissident, rioter, saboteur, enemy, insurrectionist or rebel.

When subjects revolt they openly express their dissatisfaction with the established government or policies. When such an expression is armed and organized it becomes a rebellion. When a rebellion has a large measure of support and aims to overthrow the government a state of insurgency exists.
A prediction or assessment resulting from the collection, evaluation, analysis, integration and interpretation of all available information.

One of the methods of disseminating intelligence given in a set sequence to ensure that no important details are omitted. The intelligence briefing must include 'Comment' and an overall summary of enemy capabilities. The complete format is contained in appropriate service manuals appertaining to 'Intelligence'.

This is the process by which information is turned into intelligence and disseminated. It consists of 5 stages which, although cyclical in nature, may also take place concurrently. They are summarised as follows:
a. Direction. The commander produces his intelligence requirements.
b. Tasking. The G2 staff task appropriate sources and agencies with specific questions.
c. Collection. Sources and agencies collect information or provide intelligence.
d. Processing. Information is collated, evaluated, analysed, integrated and interpreted by the G2 staff. The product of this processing is intelligence.
e. Dissemination. Information and intelligence are passed or presented to those who need it.

A written appreciation by the intelligence staff considered solely from the enemy's point of view. The intelligence staff must therefore 'think as the enemy thinks'. The estimate is made assuming the worst case, i.e., that the enemy is aware of our capabilities and intentions. The aim is to ultimately arrive at the most probable enemy COA in the given circumstance.

IPB is a systematic and continuous process of analyzing environment in a specific geographic area and the threat. IPB identifies critical battlefield decision points, so that Reconnaissance, Intelligence, Surveillance and Target Acquisition (RISTA) assets can be used to best effect, in order to assist the commander in making his decision. IPB has 3 main steps; these are battlefield area evaluation, threat evaluation and threat integration.

A non-routine report, initiated at any level, containing urgent information or intelligence that cannot await the next routine report. Whenever an interpretation of the information given in the message is included, it should be preceded by the word 'Comment'.

A routine report initiated at brigade and above levels and contains all important items of information and intelligence within the period covered, including relevant negative information. It has no format except that:
a. The text of an INTSUM is preceded by the abbreviation INTSUM.
b. The intelligence staff's deduction is preceded by the word 'Comments'.
Intelligence, Surveillance, Target Acquisition and Reconnaissance (ISTAR)

An integrated military doctrine and system, combining sensors, IT, and personnel to gather, process and distribute operational intelligence.
See also "Reconnaissance Intelligence, Surveillance, Target Acquisition (RISTA)".
Interception is the act of searching for, listening to and recording radio communications and electronic transmissions for the purpose of obtaining information.

A condition which exists when two or more items possess such functional and physical characteristics as to be equivalent in performance and durability, and are capable of being exchanged one for the other without alteration of the items or of adjoining items, except for adjustment and without selection for fit and performance.
Internal communications, by telephone or radio. May be within a HQ, an establishment, or a vehicle.
Actions to divert, disrupt, delay, or destroy the enemy before he can affect friendly forces.
The common bdry between a system or mode of op and a different system or mode.

Firing across another subunit's weapon fire. The aim is to ensure that the arcs of responsibility of the small arms of neighbouring subunits cross in order to avoid leaving a gap between sub units. Overlapping fire on the other hand takes care of the neighbouring subunits frontages.
In land warfare, an area or feature between the line of departure and an objective which must be seized or held.
A delaying position temporarily occupied by troops to cover a withdrawal and buy time to allow for the preparation and occupation of a new main defensive position.

Any military role which involves primarily the maintenance and restoration of law and order and essential services in the face of civil disturbances and disobedience, using minimum force. It covers action dealing with minor civil disorders with no political undertones as well as riots devouring of revolts and even the early stages of rebellion.
Fixed and portable systems extensively used for speech and data transmission in non-hostile operations, e.g., humanitarian relief ops.

The ability of systems, units or forces to provide services to and accept services from other systems, units or forces and to use the services so exchanged to enable them to operate effectively together.
Questioning, mainly of POWs and suspects.
Those tanks in an infantry/tank attack which assault the objective with the infantry from a fire base using direct fire.
Offensive air operations by day or night over enemy territory with the primary object of destroying enemy aircraft in the vicinity of their bases.
Flooding of an area to create an obstacle.
To lay a siege or dominate an area with a force and isolate it.

A tactical task given to a unit to seal off, both physically and psychologically, an enemy from his sources of support, deny him freedom of movement, and prevent his unit from having contact with other enemy forces.
Used by French speaking countries and means D-Day.
Jamming is the use of powerful transmissions to overwhelm an enemy receiver such that it is unable to receive wanted signals.

Javelin is a shoulder launched anti-aircraft system designed to intercept directly attacking targets. It has a minimum range of 500m, maximum ranges of 4.5 kms (against approaching aircraft) and 5.5 kms (against hovering helicopters) and a maximum effective height of 3,000 feet. It can only be fired dismounted and can only be used by day. The recent introduction of ADAD has significantly improved the early warning and target acquisition capability of Javelin detachments.

The movement of tanks to alternative positions in order to:
a. Avoid detection.
b. Avoid being engaged.
c. Gain some other tactical advantage.

A JAAT operation is a coordinated attack involving a combination of aviation and OAS aircraft, normally supported by artillery or naval gunfire and, where possible, by Electronic Warfare (EW) assets. The combination of these elements provides a highly mobile force with a destructive capability which, if used correctly, can considerably influence the course of the ground battle. The purpose of a JAAT is to provide a commander with a flexible combination of firepower that can be utilised quickly across the battlefield.
A force made up of more than one service (Army, Navy and Air force). In a CRW environment the police are inclusive.
Operations involving more than one service (Army, Navy and Air force). This includes the police in a CRW setting.
Designated point at which in all types of combat units/fmns must make contact for control and coordination.
The day on which the convoy system is introduced on any particular convoy lane.

1. A concentrated site or installation, the destruction or capture of which would seriously affect the war effort or the success of operations, e.g., ammunition dump.

2. In IS operation KPs are the priority Vulnerable Point (VP) which is classified as key and for which a military guard should be provided. The classification may be for a limited period only. Examples are:
a. Communication centre.
b. Joint HQs.
c. Public utilities such as power stations and waterworks.
d. Bridge essential to the security forces.

A key terrain is any feature or area which the seizure or control offers a marked tactical advantage. Examples of key terrain features incl: bridges, fording site, high ground, choke points, road junctions and survey control points.

An area in which a commander plans to force the enemy to concentrate, so as to destroy him with conventional or tactical nuclear weapons. The area or zones where nuclear weapons are primarily planned to be used are termed nuclear killing zones (NKZ).
A knoll is a low detached hill.

a. The time when troops cross the start line for phase 2 in a phased attack. L-Hour is therefore to be associated with attacks that are of more than one phase.
b. In amphibious and airmobile operations, L-Hour is the time at which the first helicopter of a heliborne assault wave touches down in the landing zone.

A land force consists of combat, combat support, combat service support and command support elements. The proportion of each will vary between campaigns and operations.

a. Combat Element. Combat elements are those elements that engage the enemy directly; they fight, typically employing direct-fire weapons. They include infantry, armoured and some aviation units.

b. Combat Support Element. Combat Support is 'fire support and operational assistance provided to combat elements'. Combat Support elements include: Arty fire support, air defence, reconnaissance, combat engineer, some aviation and some electronic warfare elements.

c. Combat Service Support. Combat Service Support is 'the support provided to combat forces primarily in the fields of administration and logistics'. These force elements include logistic, medical and equipment support; personnel welfare; and administration. Others are force support engineers; they provide water and electrical power supply, construct infrastructure and maintain supply routes.

d. Command Support Element. Command Support elements assist commanders in the exercise of command. They include staff of all types; communications, intelligence and information systems; and life support elements to protect, sustain and move the commander and his staff.
Seagoing craft which falls under the category of amphibious shipping, designed to carry and land forces and their equipment with or without the use of a port.
A point within a landing site where one helicopter can land.

A site within a landing zone containing one or more landing points. In amphibious operations, landing site is a continuous segment of coastline over which troops, equipment and supplies can be landed by surface means.
Any specified zone used for the landing of aircraft including troop lift aircraft.
Obstacles laid across a frontage, the aim being to cut all routes through a zone extending across the enemy's line of advance, including any lateral routes which could be used to switch axes.
The latitude of a place is the area of the meridian from the place to equator expressed in degrees at the centre of the Earth.

Temporary position occupied by one withdrawing subunit to cover the withdrawal of another. Essentially the principle of 'one leg up, one leg down', applied to withdrawal operations. It is only applicable to day withdrawal.
The art of influencing and directing men in such a manner as to obtain their willingness, loyalty, obedience and respect to accomplish a mission.

A defended formation, sometimes concealed, adopted by a force for administrative convenience and protection. Usually associated with armour. Leaguers may be close, with vehicles parked very near one another, or open, with vehicles well spaced out.

Type of tactical movement used during mechanized and non-mechanised operation. The rear vehicles/troops pass through the front vehicles/troops on to the next fire position with the latter providing covering fire. It is used where speed is essential and when enemy contact is not expected and risk can be taken.
Personnel who are exempted from full combat duty with their units.

There are 3 levels of war; they are strategic, operational, and tactical.
a. The strategic level. This includes both the grand strategy and the military strategy. Grand strategy is the application of national resources to achieve policy objectives while military strategy is the application of military resources to achieve grand strategic objectives.
b. The operational level. This extends from the level of a joint task force including the combined forces of naval, air power and ground operation to the manoeuvre brigade echelon.
c. The tactical level. This extends from the manoeuvre brigade to the lowest fighting elements including individual soldiers.

Levee en masse are inhabitants of a non-occupied territory, who on the approach of the enemy spontaneously and en masse take up arms to resist the invading forces, without having had time to form themselves into organized armed units. Participants in a "levee en masse" are considered as combatants provided they carry arms openly and must respect the law of war.

Leverage in operational art is gaining, maintaining, and exploiting advantages in combat power across all dimensions. Leverage allows joint force commanders to impose their will on the enemy, increase the enemy's dilemma, and maintain the initiative.

Liaison is defined as that contact or intercommunication maintained between elements of military forces and, where necessary, non-military agencies to ensure mutual understanding and unity of purpose and action.

A liaison officer is an officer who is exchanged between two or more forces and is empowered to represent and make appropriate recommendations on behalf of his commander. He has to be prepared to amplify his commander's intent and points of detail when appropriate. Moreover, a liaison officer shall assist his own commander through the timely exchange of information, intentions, and situational awareness.
A designated line forward of which vehicles are required to use blackout lights at night.
International armed conflicts, short of general war. It may be limited geographically, by the scale of forces or by the weapons employed but will be conducted overtly by formations of regular troops.

Type of artillery fire in which shells fall along an approximate line on any desired bearing, for example, along the line of a trench system or the front edge of a wood. This takes longer to arrange than a simple Concentration and the response to correction is slower (See "Concentration").
A form of positional defence with little or no depth.
All the land, sea, and air routes that connect an operating military force with one or more bases of operations, and along which supplies and reinforcements move.
In land warfare, a line designated to coordinate the departure of attack elements.

Lines of Logistic Support refer to the level at which logistic support is controlled. They are as follows:

a. First Line. Support integral to units; that is, A and B Echelon (see "Echelon" for details).

b. Second Line. Support within the division, less first line. This encompasses CSS at both brigade and divisional levels. In general, second line close support is found at the brigade level, while second line general support is found at the divisional level.

c. Third Line. In-theatre support to the rear of the division.
Lines of operation describe how military force is applied in time and space through decisive points on the path to the enemy centre of gravity.

Link-Up operations are conducted to join two friendly forces in enemy controlled territory. It may therefore be necessary to destroy the enemy between these forces before a link-up can be established. Both forces may be moving towards one another, or one may be stationary.

This is a location statement in the field, which must always be submitted by all units and formations immediately after every move, to the next higher HQ. A LOCSTAT must always show the exact location of the HQ originating the LOCSTAT and the HQ and/or area centre point of its subordinate formations or units. It is expressed as a six-figure grid reference.
It is the deviation of the magnetic needle of compass from its main position, owing to the presence of masses of magnetic iron ore or of iron in the neighbourhood.

Logging is the most important part of a watch keeper's job. It involves the recording of information in a prescribed manner on log sheets. The order of recording or reporting information is as follows:
a. Time (When?) - At 2220 hours.
b. Place (Where?) - At grid 654321.
c. Activity (What?) - Tank noise heard.
d. Action taken - IRONSIDE to contain.

The science of planning and carrying out the movement and maintenance of forces. Logistics in its most comprehensive sense involves those aspects of military operations which deal with:
a. Design and development, acquisition, storage, movement, distribution, maintenance, evacuation, and disposition of materiel.
b. Movement, evacuation, and hospitalisation of personnel.
c. Acquisition or construction, maintenance, operation, and disposition of facilities.
d. Acquisition or furnishing of services.
e. Medical and Health Service support.
A shortened form of instructions showing details of logistic support available to a formation.

A long message is defined as any message that will take longer than 20 seconds to transmit. Long messages are divided into convenient sections to allow for satisfactory reception in manageable stages, and to permit the transmission of more urgent traffic.
The longitude of a place is the angle at the pole between the meridian of that place and standard meridian (that of Greenwich).
Lost is a situation where the fall of shots or rounds fired by a gun, mortar or tank (main armament) is unobserved.
Low Intensity conflict is a term often used in place of Civil Disorder and Revolutionary War.
The day on which mobilization commences or is due to commence.
A store or place authorized for the storage of explosive and ammunition.
Magnetic Meridian is a magnetic NORTH and SOUTH line.
It is the angle between the true NORTH and the magnetic NORTH. It is called EAST and WEST variation according to whether the magnetic North is East or West of the true NORTH.
A large area containing the complex organization which gathers together the men and material needed to maintain the activities of armed forces engaged in war.

Main Effort is the concentration of forces or means in a particular area where a commander seeks to bring about a decision. It is a concept or 'tool' to provide a focus for the activity which a commander considers crucial to the success of his mission. The decision on where to establish the Main Effort will depend on the higher commander's Intent, the commander's mission analysis, the relative strengths and the intelligence available.
The route or routes designated within an area of operations upon which the bulk of traffic flows in support of military operations.

All supply and repair action taken to keep a force in condition to carry out its mission. It is the routine recurring work required to keep a facility (plant, building, structure, etc.) in such a condition that it may be continuously utilised, at its original or designed capacity and efficiency, for its intended purpose.

The technique of handling and controlling men in order to achieve high morale in a unit. It involves the following aspects:
a. Good leadership, including welfare of men.
b. Discipline.
c. Religion, to give troops the necessary spiritual uplifts.
d. Having an ideal, thereby 'knowing the reason why'.
e. The professional skills of the soldier.
f. Esprit-de-corps and tradition.
Employment of forces on the battlefield through movement in combination with fire, or fire potential, to achieve a position of advantage in respect to the enemy in order to accomplish the mission.
An area clear of mines or other obstacles and sufficiently wide to allow forces to manoeuvre within or pass through it, in its tactical formation.

Manoeuvre Support are those activities, primarily military engineering, which contribute to shaping the battle space to enable strategic, operational and tactical freedom of manoeuvre across the continuum of operations.

The manoeuvrist approach is that approach to operations in which shattering the enemy's overall cohesion and will to fight is paramount. It calls for an attitude of mind in which doing the unexpected, using initiative and seeking originality is combined with a ruthless determination to succeed.

A map is a plan view of the ground, drawn or not drawn to scale, showing the details existing on the ground. There are 4 types of maps; they are:
a. Cadastral Maps. These are large scale maps which cover relatively small areas, but give detailed information concerning the features of the area that is represented. Cadastral maps give details of natural features like relief, vegetation, drainage and other manmade features like settlement, communication lines, and cultivation and so on.
b. Sketch Maps. Sketch maps are in most cases rough maps not drawn to scale. They are often called plans, and drawn without regard to details of accuracy as they are often drawn freehand.
c. Distribution Maps. These are maps drawn from information obtained from geographical data, usually of such elements as weather or climate, population, crops or minerals. Distribution maps provide very useful information that can be easily interpreted and so they are very useful for the purpose of regional planning.
d. Atlas Maps. Atlas maps are small scale maps that represent very large areas ranging in size from localized region such as a local government area, to a state, a continent or even the whole world. Atlas maps cover large areas, therefore, they are drawn to small scales and they do not necessarily contain as much detailed information about the area as cadastral maps.

Martial law is a condition that exists when disorder has reached such proportions that the normal legal processes of the state cannot function any longer and the only organization that can impose any authority is the armed forces, by force of its arms. A state of martial law involves the suspension of ordinary law and its replacement by military rule.

All stores and equipment required by a force for an undertaking. It includes:

a. Combat Supplies (C Sups). See "Combat Supplies".

b. Ordnance Stores. See "Ordnance Stores".

c. Vehicles. See "Vehicles".

d. Engineer and Defence Stores.

e. Specialist Medical and Dental Equipment Stores.
Infantry borne in armoured personnel carriers (APCs), thereby gaining increased protection, added mobility and more firepower.
Form of warfare in which all the combat elements are mounted in armoured vehicles.
Mediation is when a third party assists by acting between opposed parties in an effort to bring them together.
Small medical detachment, lower to an MRS in status, which provides first line medical cover to the unit or subunit to which it is attached.

Meeting Engagement is a combat action that may occur when both sides seek to fulfil their mission by offensive action. It will often occur during an advance to contact and can easily lead to a hasty attack.

The meeting engagement differs from the advance to contact in that it occurs unexpectedly, whereas in the advance to contact, the commander is deliberately seeking to establish contact with the enemy.
Prior intention to commit a criminal act, with the knowledge that the act is a crime.
A true NORTH and SOUTH line.

A message is any thought or idea expressed briefly, in plain or coded language, and prepared in a form suitable for transmission by a means of communication.
All messages for transmission over a net radio are either:

a. Informal (or unregistered) messages.
Informal messages are transmitted either directly by the originator or passed verbally or in writing to an operator for transmission. Originators of informal messages for transmission by an operator should write their message down if verbal instructions are likely to cause error or confusion.
Written informal messages are not normally drafted on a message form, signed by the originator, or registered in a message centre. However, they are usually passed directly from the originator to the operator for transmission.

b. Formal (or registered) messages.
Formal messages are normally prepared for indirect communication between originators and addressees from different units or formations, which are served by separate radio nets or other communications systems. Consequently, the requirement for these messages on most tactical voice nets, particularly at unit level, is minimal.

A message is given a precedence to indicate the order in which it should be handled. The degrees of precedence are:

a. ROUTINE.

b. PRIORITY.

c. IMMEDIATE.

d. FLASH.

Any message which contains information that may be of value to an enemy must be classified (all others are UNCLASSIFIED). The originator is responsible for ensuring that a message bears the lowest classification consistent with its contents.

The categories are:

a. TOP SECRET.

b. SECRET.

c. CONFIDENTIAL.

d. RESTRICTED.

e. UNCLASSIFIED.
An agency responsible for acceptance, transmission, receipt and delivery of msgs.
Military Aid to the Civil Community (MACC)

MACC is the provision of tri-Service personnel and equipment both in emergencies, such as natural disasters, and in routine situations to assist the community at large. Examples of this role are the use of EOD bomb disposal units and assisting the community during a civil emergency such as flooding.
Military Aid to the Civil Ministries (MACM)

This encompasses the use of military forces for non-military government tasks, including assistance to maintain public services and the essentials of life in a community or to undertake urgent work of national importance. Recent examples include firefighting and providing emergency ambulance and prison support services.
Military Aid to the Civil Power (MACP)
MACP is the help the military provides to maintain public order and security when the police are unable to control the situation.

The personal staff officer of a two-star general or appointment of two-star general and above. The nature of duty is not as personal as that of the ADC. It involves chiefly office work and includes:
a. Supervision of work in the office.
b. Sorting out all papers addressed to the commander.
c. Preparation of notes, papers and speeches for the commander.
Military effectiveness is the standard by which the Army is judged in peace and war, from platoon to the highest levels.
Military Law is a set of rules and regulations or body of laws for the day-to-day administration of the military disciplinary control of the members of Armed Forces.

Any object which by nature, location, purpose or use makes an effective contribution to military action and whose total or partial destruction, capture or neutralisation, in the circumstances ruling at the time, offers a definite military advantage.

An explosive or material, normally encased, designed to destroy or damage ground vehicles, boats or aircraft, or designed to wound, kill or otherwise incapacitate personnel. It may be detonated by the presence, proximity or contact of a person or vehicle, i.e., it must be initiated by its intended target.
Anti-tank mines or an anti-tank mine protected by a number of anti-personnel mines or a group of anti-personnel mines.
A single row of clusters laid in a generally straight line.
Two parallel mine clusters laid simultaneously six paces apart.

In land warfare, minefield is an area of ground containing mines laid with or without a pattern. The types of minefield are:
a. Protective Minefield. Used to assist a unit in its local close protection. It is laid by the unit concerned and should be covered by direct fire.
b. Tactical Minefield. It is laid to block enemy attack formations in selected areas to deflect his approach into a favourable killing area. It is also used to prevent penetration between positions and strengthen the defence of the positions. It should be covered by direct indirect fire; it is also called barrier minefield.
c. Nuisance Minefield. It is laid to delay and disorganise the enemy and to hinder his use of an area or route. It is laid without pattern.
d. Phoney Minefield. It is used to simulate a minefield in an area with the object of deceiving the enemy. Also known as dummy minefield.
e. Defensive Minefield. This is minefield laid in accordance with an established plan to prevent penetration between positions and strengthen the defence of the positions themselves. They are laid by engineers, ahead of protective minefields.
The opening of routes through a minefield when not against enemy oppositions.
The average number of mines per metre of an area.
A portion of a minefield in which no mines have been laid, or special width, to enable a friendly force pass through in tactical formation. Normally not less than 100m wide.
An un-mined (or de-mined) route through any minefield suitably marked. Lanes will usually be classified as 'Vehicle Lanes' (8 metres wide) or 'Foot Lanes' (2 metres wide).
A complete written record of all pertinent information concerning a minefield, submitted on a standard form (AF 4017A) by the officer in charge of laying operations.

Minimum force means the minimum necessary force that is reasonable in any circumstance to achieve the immediate aim. The degree of force can never be reasonable if it is more than that required to achieve the immediate aim. Minimum necessary force does not mean minimum necessary troops. A large number of men deployed at the right time may enable a commander to use less force than he might otherwise have done.

A military command philosophy that empowers subordinate commanders to exercise initiative, make decisions and take appropriate action to accomplish an assigned mission in accordance with the superior commander's intent. The essence of Mission Command is to encourage subordinate commanders to use their initiative to accomplish the mission in accordance with the superior commander's intent.
Mission Command provides an approach to issuing orders that enables subordinates to understand the following:
a. The Commander's Intentions - What the commander is trying to achieve.
b. Their Missions - The specific effect they are expected to achieve.
c. The Purpose or Intent of Their Missions - Why they need to accomplish their missions and how they contribute to the commander's overall concept of operations.
d. Their Delegated Freedom of Action - The limits within which they are authorised to operate and exercise their initiative.
A forward air liaison agency for support helicopter commanded by an air force officer.

Mobile defence focuses on the defeat of the attacking force by permitting it to advance to a position which exposes it to counter attack and envelopment by a mobile striking force. The emphasis is on destroying the enemy rather than retaining or retaking ground.
Mobile reserves are troops earmarked for ejecting an enemy force that has penetrated a defensive locality/area.

1. The act of preparing for war or other emergencies through assembling and organising national resources.

2. The process by which the armed forces or part of it are brought to a state of readiness for war or other national emergency. It includes organizing personnel, supplies and materiel for active military service. It may involve the call up of reservists.
Mobility is the capability of forces to move from one place to another whilst retaining the ability to fulfil their mission. Speed of movement is what is significant in manoeuvre warfare.

MC is an open area through which a force can manoeuvre in accordance with its tactical doctrine. It is categorized according to the size of unit or formation which can manoeuvre through them. MC may contain "Slow Go" areas.
Modulation is the process by which the amplitude, freq or phase of a carrier wave is varied with time in accordance with the wave form of superimposed information, e.g., speech.
A simple petrol bomb. An improvised explosive device usually made of a bottle filled with a flammable liquid such as petrol and a wick that is set alight just before it is thrown.
Momentum, in military terms, is a measure of the effect that a formation or unit that is moving can have. It is the product of that moving force's size and speed.

The time planned for the explosion of the first of a series of tactical nuclear weapons as part of a specified ground forces operation (or in the case of a single strike, the time planned for that explosion).

In conducting IPB, a NAI is an area which will confirm or deny enemy intentions. It serves to focus attention on areas where the enemy must appear if he has chosen a particular course of action (COA). NAIs provide an objective basis for the employment of RISTA assets. Depending on the amount of ground being observed, there may be Point NAIs, e.g., cross-roads, or Area NAIs, e.g., a valley.
A table showing when enemy activity may be expected in each NAI and the type of activity expected.
Direction finding to get to a given point or place.
Negotiations take place when two parties with opposing views meet to resolve their differences.

A net identification sign (NIS) is a random, twice-daily-changing, two-letter group (with the exception of CC) allotted to a radio net to provide a concealed reference to the identity of that net. The NIS should be used whenever it is necessary to distinguish between radio nets or, in conjunction with a call sign, to identify a station on a specific net.
The organization in an FTX that deals with exercise casualties with regards to men, vehicles and equipment and the handling of tokens used to represent real stores.
A 'neutral State' is a State formally or in fact not party to a given armed conflict.
Neutralise is to punish a target with fire in order to render it ineffective. Neutralization does not necessarily imply destruction.

A nickname consists of two words neither of which must be a colour. It is used for convenience to refer to a particular matter in which security protection is not required, e.g., a report line. The two words to be paired should each be distinct and not normally associated to avoid being mistaken for a Code word. Bad examples are 'WRIST' with 'WATCH' or 'MATCH' with 'BOX'.

A nick number consists of a two-figure number, used to provide low grade security and easy reference to geography locations. Nick numbers are most useful in mobile operations but not in static positions. They should not be used for location states.
NVP is the plan by which all-night surveillance devices are coordinated over the battle area.

An area into which no fire support or the effects of fire support are allowed, except:

a. When the establishing HQ temporarily approves fire missions within the NFA on a mission-by-mission basis; or

b. When an enemy force within the NFA engages a friendly force. In this case, the commander may engage the enemy to defend his force.

See also "No Fire Line".

A NFL is a line short of which artillery, aircraft or ships do not fire except on request or approval of the supported commander, but beyond which they may fire at any time without danger to friendly troops.

See also "No Fire Area".

"No Go" areas are grounds over which manoeuvre of a deployed force is considered impracticable. It must be assessed according to the type of force; for example, armour, wheeled and dismounted forces have different requirements and constraints.
That area of ground between two opposing forces which is not physically occupied by either, but which both will endeavour to dominate by means of patrols, observation and similar methods.

A procedure employed during training exercises to transmit 'real' messages which are not part of the exercise. The word NODUF is entered in the MESSAGE INSTRUCTIONS box and also at the beginning of the text. For example, if a participant in an exercise gets badly injured and a helicopter is needed for medevac, such a message will be a 'NODUF' message.

A night attack where all available fire support is used. This method is employed when there is little chance of achieving surprise by stealth or when it is expedient in the circumstances. Deception measures should be planned nevertheless, to conceal the place, scope, direction and timing of the assault.
A NEO is a raid which involves incursion into, and temporary occupation of territory for the purpose of rescuing non-combatants and ends with a planned withdrawal.

Those troops, vehicles and equipment that are determined undesirable or not required during the conduct of a withdrawal operation and should be got rid of early. They are the first elements to withdraw after the Rear Recce Party and may include elements such as cooks, regimental aid post, etc.
